title: Videogame board games have a new crown jewel, and it's Kingdom Come Deliverance
content:
Our Verdict

Kingdom Come Deliverance: The Board Game is worth your time, whether you've played the videogames or not. It's an interesting, efficient deck-building puzzle that, at the same time, gives you space to stop and smell the flowers (or enjoy its storylines). Learning to play this huge, token-laden behemoth is an uphill battle, and four-player games take 5+ hours to tackle. But, if you can forgive its few minor hiccups, you're in for a fantastic time.

Pros
  • Endless variety
  • Beautiful components
  • Wonderful blend of strategy and story
  • Clever, efficient deck-building
  • Authentic homage to the game
Cons
  • A slog to learn
  • Runs extremely long with more than two players
  • One or two clunky mechanics

I can't stop comparing Kingdom Come Deliverance: The Board Game to Gloomhaven (or, perhaps more fittingly, Mage Knight). It's less about shared mechanics, though, and more about feeling.

Here is a sprawling, component-heavy board game that takes longer to set up than many take to play. Here is a game that marries euro-style strategy gameplay with adventure stories, with little compromise on either side. Here is a board game where sessions last for hours, and you might never run out of new things to discover. Here is a board game that'll soar to the top of many players' Game of the Year lists.

Kingdom Come Deliverance: The Board Game is a triumph, if only because it's a videogame board game I actually want to play. It's a rare treasure that celebrates its source material with authenticity, but never forgets that board games are a fundamentally different medium. Videogame board games often think the truest representation of their original IP is clunky, grindy gameplay. Kingdom Come, in contrast, is as smooth as freshly churned butter.

It might not seem that way on your first playthrough. The rulebook is 50+ pages, and designers Vlaada Chvátil (Galaxy Trucker, Mage Knight) and Tomáš Holek (SETI) have a lot of interlocking mechanics to explain. Here's a little summary.

KCDTBG (as I'm calling it now, because that title is a mouthful) is a competitive adventure game that's primarily powered by deck-building. You spend five days - each with four turns - exploring the kingdom of Bohemia, with the aim of having more victory points than your mates by the end.

There's a small serving of point salad here, with many paths to a high score. Your main methods can be boiled down to three activities: upgrading your deck, completing quests, and acquiring pricey items.

We'll dive into your deck first. Everyone starts with a basic deck of cards, and each card has three uses. You can discard a card to reap the rewards of its bottom text, which usually increases the movement track on your player board. You'll need this to wander the fields and towns of Bohemia.

Moving is one of many minor actions you can perform on your turn, provided you can pay for it. Other 'free' actions include visiting shops, washing in troughs, rearranging your inventory, and consuming food (there are penalties for getting too hungry).

You only get one main action per turn, and only three per day (your fourth must be spent 'resting', which replenishes your resources). Main actions come in six categories: hunting, stealing, fighting, 'befriending', herb gathering, and training. Those first four have specific colors and icons to them.

To perform an action, you must play a card from your hand. If the center text of the card shows that action's related symbol, you play the card face up, gaining the benefits of said middle text. You can still play a card if it lacks the right symbol, but it's played face-down, with no additional reward.

Then, you must complete a test to see whether your action succeeds. You'll draw and discard cards from your deck (usually three, but sometimes more or less), and this time, you pay attention to the text at the top of the card. Draw cards with enough symbols matching the test type (or universal gold success symbols), and you succeed!

Obviously, success becomes more likely if you have better cards in your deck. Advanced cards offer more success symbols, as well as unique powers to influence tests. Plus, you score points for adding advanced cards to your deck, plus for any you retire.

You usually retire cards through a training action or as a reward for other activities (such as placing beds after a successful befriending action). As for acquiring cards, your best bet is to climb the skill tracks on the left of your player board. You'll pick up skills on your adventures, and once you've got enough, you can spend them on a card of your choice from the tableau.

But wait, how do you increase your skills?! It's time to talk about point-scorer number two: quests.

Quests garnish your deck-building with a little narrative. Some are minor affairs picked up in taverns, while others are involved, multi-step parts of a greater story. The requests are myriad. One day, you might be brewing remedies for the sick; another sees you digging up corpses to pilfer their jewelry. Many of these story beats are loving nods to the videogame, but you don't need any prior experience to enjoy them.

A quest's rewards are as diverse as the quests themselves. Some, as I mentioned, offer skill tree increases. Others might place beds, netting you the points and one-time benefits associated. Others simply promise cold, hard cash.

Groschen is a wonderful thing in KCDTBG. Every 10 groschen is worth a point by itself, but its purchasing power is often more valuable. You can buy resources that would have otherwise been time-consuming to gather: food, flowers, and even beds. From merchants, you can buy horses, armor, clothing, weapons, and tchotchke (with a steep discount, if you've already befriended them).

Horses and gear often come with symbols that count as extra successes in specific tests. Some weapons even allow you to draw more cards when hunting and fighting - neat! Neatest of all are the padlock symbols on these cards and tokens. For every two of those you have equipped at game-end, you score one point.

There's our gameplay loop in a (rather long) nutshell. You wander the map, completing quests to increase your wealth and abilities. The aim is to gather as many positive resources as you can (advanced cards, groschen, 'good' cards for moral acts, and material goods) while reducing the number of negative resources in your pool (dirt, wounds, hunger, and 'evil' cards acquired through morally bankrupt deeds).

With so many moving parts, learning to play is an uphill battle, even with tutorial videos and a well-designed starter scenario. At an estimated 80 minutes per player, KCDTBG already moves at a glacial page, and that's before we factor in return trips to the rulebook.

Regardless, that first game leaves you hungry, and pacing improves with additional games. It's not long before you can marvel at how cleverly efficient the deck-building is, and how endlessly replayable it seems.

Gloomhaven keeps players engaged for years on end with hundreds of different story scenarios. KCDTBG only has a handful of main story quests, but combine these with a chunky deck of side quests, plus four decks of advanced cards to build with, and you've got a game that never feels the same. CGE's previous board game, Drillers, had fans immediately demanding expansions to keep gameplay fresh, but Kingdom Come scarcely needs support.

It's not all roses, of course. The fighting action is bogged down by a clunky, unnecessarily complex combat mini-game. And even this otherwise seamless system doesn't feel quite strong enough to justify games that last five, six, or more hours.

KCDTBG comes close to earning those all-day sessions, but its strategy isn't quite rich enough to keep me enthralled that long. Three players is the most I'd want to play with, or perhaps less - because all low player counts miss is a breadth of stories.

Perhaps part of this struggle at high player counts is how solitary gameplay is. There's a 'meeting' mechanic that gives players perks for sharing a space, and main storylines often present a race to earn the best rewards. Other than this, player interaction is ignored. A four-player game feels very much like a one- or two-player one, only with double the runtime.

Still, these are only small flecks of dirt on the game's shiny armor. This is an excellent game from two of board gaming's star designers. You don't need to have played the videogame to love it, though you will need a high tolerance for long, hefty games with hordes of fiddly pieces.

Want to learn more about the year's best board games? We update our guide with weekly reviews, or we can recommend you our favorites in the Wargamer Discord.

A review copy of this game was provided by the publisher.

title: Magic: The Gathering Star Trek Review, Part 3 of 4 – White, Blue, & Black Cards
content:
Space, the final frontier. These are the voyages of the starship Enterprise...as well as around 34 other new Spaceraft. Our continuing mission: To explore in detail the ramifications of newly-printed cardboard; to speculate upon their effects on formats such as Commander, Standard, & Modern; to boldly joke about the 43 new Creature types printed in this set unlikely ever to be seen again! Yes, Star Trek has arrived to Magic, and with it a host of new cards sure to shake things up. Most impactful is the full realization of Spacecraft as an Artifact subtype, more than doubling the number thusly printed. Today we're covering the set's white, blue, and black cards.

Star Trek officially releases to tabletop on November 13th, and on Magic: The Gathering Arena on November 10th.

White

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Brad Boimler, Eager Ensign

Saffgor: The key thing to note about Brad is that as written (and clarified in the release notes) twiddling this gentleman results in cumulative replacement effects, meaning you can very readily get to a point where you're putting 3-5 extra counters on your permanents when you do so. That's compelling for such a low cost, and White has exceptional ways to do that, so I'm gonna mark this as an early runner for sleeper hit in the set, maybe worthy of a full article.

BPhillipYork: Adding more counters is nice, and with things like charge counters for Spacecraft it's relatively easy to tap him for some other benefit. With beam up you could easily beam him up, drop him back down and tap him again for something else, even just more charge counters on a Spacecraft, or mount something, or crew a Vehicle. He also plays really well with blink effects. Adding a bunch more counters onto a card is particularly dangerous with planeswalkers, since they can come out fully charged up, and create an emblem or use an ultimate ability right away.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Captain Jean-Luc Picard

Saffgor: If you abstract Picard, he's essentially Creature-based Magda that finds Legendary Creatures, by way of chain-tutoring for The Seriema, or if you're feeling spicy, Deep Space 9. Between those two options you can build a spooky board, flicker for combo pieces, and more...but getting there is far more telegraphed & mana-intensive than Magda. He's strong, but probably not cEDH strong.

BPhillipYork: As a mono-white commander I'm not sure that's terribly exciting, but as an anthem for a creature heavy deck it's kind of nuts. To be honest, you've got a creature that makes token creatures and buffs all creatures and lets you fetch something that'll likely be turned into it's creature form pretty fast, which is all really useful in a 3-cost creature.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Conquest Mission

Saffgor: This is pretty easy to fuel up, and starts letting you go pretty wide pretty fast. In the decks that want Artifact Creature bodies, seems like a slam dunk.

BPhillipYork: This is just strong. Like, dumping out mana rocks gets you 1/1s. That's super dangerous amounts of easy token creature creation.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Command Subadjunct

Saffgor: This doesn't look exciting, but a lot of the best Artifact Creatures have tap abilities, and this allows you to swing out before pushing for that...or beat your own stax pieces which would otherwise prevent untapping.

BPhillipYork: Diet Sliver effect is a useful buff for your artifact creatures, but most likely you're just running this for yet another Borg.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Dr. Beverly Crusher

Saffgor: I don't love this design. Sure she gets big, sure it doubles triggers, but this feels like the most whitebread way to build for a lifegain payoff. It's bland, and without tremendous depth.

BPhillipYork: Well double life gain triggers is useful for decks that run a lot of life gain triggers, and they are super easy to generate a ton of triggers off of. It's good leverage, you just need a plan for it.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Dr. McCoy, Surly Surgeon

Saffgor: Helps counter-based decks beat boardwipes, yeah sure I'm down. It's a hair expensive, and would have preferred Flash, but I could see this working.

BPhillipYork: There's plenty of ways to leverage this to be useful, and if you have a way to distribute +1/+1 counters at instant speed it lets you avoid most removal. For 4 mana though and it removing all the +1/+1 counters it gets a little weird. Most decks that want +1/+1 counters want a lot of them, and this will remove all of them. It also prevents the destruction, rather than dying and coming back, which would be a lot more useful.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Excalbian Gamemaster

Saffgor: 6 mana isn't where you want to be for any of this Creature's text, but it's a Mythic because it wins hard in limited. Meh.

BPhillipYork: This isn't super exciting. If you're maxing out on differently named lands, that's a lot of effort just to get a lot of 1/1s.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Federation Resupply

Saffgor: Wow, they really kicked Open the Armory to the curb? This is absolutely tremendous, and even the self-bounce can help you double up on your enter effects, which White so often has. Amazing card, and you'll see this everywhere, although between the name and keyword reprinting it seems difficult for a card with such likely ubiquity.

BPhillipYork: There's not a ton of Equipment tutors so this is useful there, and pretty nice to also be able to grab an Aura or a Spacecraft. Tutors are pretty much always good, particularly ones you can use twice.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Miles O'Brien, Transporter Ops

Saffgor: Self-bounce payoff makes sense in White, but I do worry the actual payoff of drawing a card is only okay, compared to the need to recast whatever's being bounced. Yes you can just do it with free Artifacts, but if Bennie Bracks, Zoologist has taught me anything it's that slow engines like this in White usually do less than you'd hope.

BPhillipYork: I like the interaction with beam me up, but there's not really enough ways to beam things up to make a deck around this, particularly in mono-white. So while I think you could build around this, I don't know that I would really recommend it.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

The Needs of the Many

Saffgor: A worse Everybody Lives!, and probably a worse Flare of Fortitude. No thanks.

BPhillipYork: This is pretty great. Having another source of this sort of effect makes it a lot more consistent in a 100 card deck, and the immunity to damage is pretty great with spells like Earthquake, letting you run some damage based mass-removal.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Peace in Our Time

Saffgor: Well hello conspicuous win condition for the aforementioned Brad Boimler! The fact you can skip combat the turn this comes down is essential, but it being an upkeep win is what scares me. Could definitely work, but it's fragile.

BPhillipYork: This seems like it really won't work that well. Who is ever going to let it get to 12? Players will draw some cards early and then just start attacking you, or stop drawing the cards. There's definitely ways to proliferate, so you could get a few counters then turbo it out yourself, but that seems like a lot of steps for a weird win-con that can also just be destroyed.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Sulu, Space Swashbuckler

Saffgor: As a huge fan of George Takei, I can tell you right now this card makes me a bit mad. That saying, 'oh my'—that's from an appearance on Howard Stern, and not any episode of Star Trek. To see it appear on the card for Sulu, a character he plays, is weird. Anyway, card is fine, it's a better but less interesting Brad Boimler.

BPhillipYork: This seems fairly weak for a pretty memorable moment in Star Trek.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

There's Coffee in that Nebula

Saffgor: This isn't too far off of being a White Stock Up, and given how good that card is I'm inclined to rate this pretty highly! Very neat card in decks with 3cmc or less combo pieces.

BPhillipYork: For Commander this is probably not going to rate, searching the top for a combo piece is probably insufficient and there are tons of better plains tutors out there, even if you can use it twice.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Troubling Tribbles

Saffgor: Worse Scute Swarm, cannot bring myself to get excited about this.

BPhillipYork: Well that's fun. A nice reference, and for maybe life gain decks it could be useful, but 3 CMC is probably too much. If you could drop it on turn 2 I think that would make a big difference. Maybe if you're generating extra upkeeps or extra turns, but there's really more fun things to so this ends up sort of being just a meme card.

Blue

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

The Caretaker

Saffgor: This looks incredible until you look for repeatable means of facing dilemmas, and it's...scant. Arguably the most accessible is stuff like Pyramids, and that's not an exciting Magic card. This falls short until they print better Dilemma enablers.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Data, New Life

Saffgor: This is cheap as hell for the effect, whoa. Gets out of hand fast, and comes down early enough to get out of hand. Legendary matters here, because if it weren't you could jam multiple turn 2/3 in a tempo shell in Standard, I reckon.

BPhillipYork: He's generally going to get decently big fast, but in Commander who really cares. No evasion, and what you have to draw about 30 cards before he's really going to be threatening, if you can draw 30 cards you can probably do something useful rather than just uh, swing out with a big creature. Maybe in a wheel deck.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Dominion Saboteur

Saffgor: This is clearly meant to copy Spacecraft, but at 5 mana I just don't buy it. 4 would have been the sweet spot.

BPhillipYork: This is a neat twist on a copy spell. Artifact or creature and entering with counters does give you some interesting possibilities, so I think it is definitely useful to copy certain commanders or certain key artifacts, or if Time Vault was legal maybe, oh I see they oracled that again. But even so, it's a bit of an expansion to be nonlegendary and have counters, which is useful.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Gwyndala, the Progeny

Saffgor: So this is why all those Communicators copy themselves! Gwyndala is a frontrunner for the most popular Monocolor option in the set, and it's not hard to see why; she makes fantastic use of blink, token copiers, and even some weird cards like Brass Knuckles, all in service of suiting up with multiple copies of Colossus Hammer or Swords of X & Y. She's great, and probably worth a full article of coverage!

BPhillipYork: I don't know what exactly you'd copy to make this really good. Paying 4 mana to get a temporary copy of an Equipment is probably not really going to do that much that 1 copy of it wouldn't do, and it's all kinds of slow and telegraphed, itching for removal.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

H.M.S. Bounty, Unlikely Timeship

Saffgor: We've arrived to my favorite card of the set, and of all things it's a Whale typal enabler...or more appropriately, a 'deck with Whales' enabler. I covered the Bounty in one of our most extensive Commander Focus articles in a while, but to put it bluntly there's a shocking depth to the Whale Creature type, and being able to find them allows for one of the most fun, compelling, & resilient combo lists I've played in years. This card sparks joy.

BPhillipYork: Whale tutor is fun, and taking an extra turn is fun also. Pretty easy to get the extra turn with just a random changeling. Well templated to avoid any kind of abuse.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Jett Reno, Problem Solver

Saffgor: Jett does some neat things by way of the few repeatable Dilemma enablers, and she can be a solid value engine in any deck looking for a way to Station. Quietly pretty decent, and has some weird combos with Agatha's Soul Cauldron & Cryptic Trilobite.

BPhillipYork: This is fine for like, dilemma deck I guess, other than that, it's really meh.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Lieutenant Commander Data

Saffgor: In Star Trek, we received a fantastic 3 mana Creature value engine I expect to see play in a number of formats. Her name is Nyota Uhura, Communications. In a huge twist I'm actually pretty bearish on this version of Data, because unlike a Cabbage Merchant or Remora, you need to actually pay for your value. I prefer mine incidental, thanks very much, but Data does have one upside as a Saga Creature/Persist Commander, and I think if you play him in the Command Zone you can have a good time there.

BPhillipYork:  He's probably going to get big fast, and you can make him less threatening but turning that into draw. It's a pretty fun mechanic, that also makes for a decent, though similarly non-evasive beater.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Kobayashi Maru Scenario

Saffgor: The fact this is being printed into a Standard with Harmless Offering and a new card we'll talk about shortly is interesting. I think this can...actually get there, so long as the format slows down on aggro enough to allow for this to hit the final option. Four dilemmas too, that's something to note.

BPhillipYork: Not sure I love the proliferation of "lose the game" type enchantments into more colors. There is a sort of neat thing with trading or giving these away, and blue has Donate already and there's getting to be more and more ways to hand out permanent "gifts", which, this is one where you'd probably want to look it in the mouth. It's also such an iconic thing from Star Trek they sort of had to do it.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Lt. Cmdr. Geordi La Forge

Saffgor: In the right deck this is a great accelerant, but there's a lot of similar effects which do more for around the same cost.

BPhillipYork: This is just a huge enabler for a charge counter deck, really kind of dangerous and there are a lot of charge counters around. As a commander you probably can't really leverage it enough in mono-blue, but as just an additional card these sorts of decks. Pretty fun for just pure Spaceship tribal.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Mr. Spock, Science Officer

Saffgor: Teferi's Ageless Insight, but unlocked and on a body. Yeah, I'm down for that; they managed to make this card exciting with just a single line of text.

BPhillipYork: Okay well that's a decent draw card, fat butt so resistant to damage. Doubling draw is nice but it's often a bit of a win-more kind of thing, unless you have a deck that has a way to really use all those cards you're drawing. Otherwise it really just ends up being card selection.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Nyota Uhura, Communications

Saffgor: Talion's little sister, and she's looking great! Blocks a lot of attackers profitably in the Tymna matchup, cheaper, and while you do lose the P/T mattering I'm not especially sad about that. If you wanted to play Pollywog Prodigy, but didn't have the bodies to get it to ~3 power, Uhura is here to save you, and look great doing it.

BPhillipYork: There's getting to be an awful lot of cards like this, letting you choose and locking down numbers, and potentially you end up drawing all the time. Which is good. Most of the time, at a good table, throwing this on like 1 is going to net you a lot of cards, though you have to know your table.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Open Communications

Saffgor: The cost of entry for a self-bounce here is so, so low, and if you're in a playgroup where Darksteel Mutation and the like run rampant, please consider playing this card. It will rarely feel amazing, but never feel bad.

BPhillipYork: This seems fine. It's probably almost just another cantrip most of the time and you probably won't end up beaming it up, so for cantrip decks it's always nice to have more ways, especially given how many cards there are that generate mana off casts now.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Rules of Acquisition

Saffgor: 2 of this, 4 Harmless Offering, Kobayashi Maru Scenario. Standard. Someone's gotta make it work.

BPhillipYork: I feel like they could've made a whole set out of these, and it would've been a fun set. Ferengi Secret Lair. But I think the real winner here is the give away, since you can give away something value less or even dangerous and get draw, which is pretty nice. It's slow but fun.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Scotty, Miracle Worker

Saffgor: This is some of the worst templating I've seen for what is ostensibly a clear effect. The reason everything gains Beam Me Up is so it works with Adventures, essentially, but that use case isn't worth overcomplicating the effect. Card is fine, wording is atrocious.

BPhillipYork: I'm a little shocked he doesn't give cards miracle in some way, though that isn't really a set mechanic. Beam me up all the time is great if you're doing something abusive with it, constantly returning something for value. With artifact draw and cost reduction all over blue this could easily be a combo enabler in the Command Zone, that also generates a ton of value while you're getting to the combo stage.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Those Old Scientists

Saffgor: I think the art style on this as the main printing for a card is unacceptable. Just, straight up, this isn't okay as the only art for the card to come in. Imagine if this was a staple, especially given other characters from the show have been rendered in Magic's normal style.

BPhillipYork: In terms of power level this is fine, frankly Lower Decks was the best Star Trek show, and I'm sad it isn't on more cards.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Seven of Nine, Unassimilated

Saffgor: This being a Mythic is very odd to me, because the card seems...bad? Like, not even mediocre, straight up bad. 0/4 that loots until you're into the late game isn't where we are right now, in terms of game pace, and the Melvin-esque 7/9 ability reeks of an forced joke.

BPhillipYork: Okay, this is fun I guess. I mean it's card draw on 2 mana which is selection really, but discard can be leveraged decently, and then you can make it big, though like who cares. I'm not sure why they didn't go with the iconic catsuit though, the one that got Obama elected.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Vulcan Mind-Meld

Saffgor: Really fantastic with anything that cares about casting from outside of your hand, or in Commander where you can dole out a card to someone you politic with. I love this card, and while it isn't meant for 60-card formats that's okay.

BPhillipYork: This is kind of dangerous, I mean you're really giving away 2 cards for one, but there's lots of ways to lock out casting from exile, or benefit from casting from exile that make it probably worth while.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Wesley Crusher, Starfleet Cadet

Saffgor: I spent many nights as a tween watching TableTop with Wil Wheaton, so forgive me my affection for the man, where so many lack it. Wesley's pretty neat! You get a Cryptic Command-ish on a body that faces a Dilemma on ETB and helps you tempo forward.

BPhillipYork: This seems fine, basically an already existing card that is now on a body. There's a bit of modality that could be useful here, but there's probably two modes (top two) that are the big plays almost all the time, though draw discard isn't too bad.

Black

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Blastoneuron

Saffgor: Lot of clones that cost 3 or less, you know. I think there's a reasonable Pioneer deck which runs this and cheap clones to force a win by stacking Blastoneurons, but that might be too cute. Card does seem strong though, and there's reasonable targets across formats.

BPhillipYork: The trigger is huge there, the animation of a token is fine, though usually reanimation decks want to recur things repeatedly, as opposed to a single shot.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Collation Trimatrix

Saffgor: Remember that Vigilance granter earlier up? This is his buddy. Cryptbreaker is the closest analogy, and that card was pretty good back in the day.

BPhillipYork: Wow. That's pretty bonkers. Amazing for token artifact creature decks, Borg decks, some Phyrexian decks, Myr decks, etc..

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Death is Irrelevant

Saffgor: You're only ever cheating this out, but if you do it presents some fair-but-fun problems for the table. Hardcasting this is a pipe dream though.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

The Destruction of Praxis

Saffgor: This seems pretty darn good in 60-card formats, and getting to that 6+ effect isn't hard even in Standard.

BPhillipYork: Board clear that is -X/-X is really good since it tends to sweep right past all the normal board protection cards. Keying it off your land types is fine, you generally won't need to hit more than -4 or -5 toughness in any case.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Georgiou, Terran Emperor

Saffgor: Obvious funny card with this is as a way to draw the deck with Ad Nauseam, but there's a lot of ways to break a Lich effect in the Command Zone. At 6 mana it's a hair expensive and fragile, but I see the appeal.

BPhillipYork: I love the idea of a balls out deck that wants to sit around at 0 or less life and generating hordes of 1/1 red Officer creature tokens. I mean, they aren't particularly good tokens but it's such a funny deck idea, so inherently bad, that it's kind of awesome.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Gul Dukat, Colonial Prefect

Saffgor: Functionally double your damage, then gain a ton of life—this is a Timmy payoff if ever I saw one. Three Black pips does make it appealing for devotion purposes, though.

BPhillipYork: Well that's a brutal life loss / gain trigger. For 7 mana it would have to be, but even so, just something like Pestilence is going to go insane with this. I would say it's almost too dangerous, especially since it's every end step. Still throwing this down and going unanswered will probably end the game pretty quickly.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Khan, Vengeful Heart

Saffgor: As someone who greatly enjoys Eternal Scourge (It's among my three favorite Magic cards), seeing another card of its ilk brings me great joy. Thank goodness Khan isn't Green, as that does restrict his utility with Food Chain lines, but even so he remains a powerful combo piece, and likely the best card like Scourge to date.

BPhillipYork: Cards that can be cast from exile are really kind of weird. Weird tricks with Food Chain are the default sort of BS here, but black also has some triggers from exile that this guy could be used to abuse. At 4 mana it's really tricky to anything aside from Food Chain unless you're willing to invest in some cost reduction.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Overflow Submatrix

Saffgor: Extremely safe design with a lot of guardrails, but the fact some aggro Artifact Creature deck might exist in Standard means this could see play at 1-2 copies.

BPhillipYork: Well recurring your lost creatures is always useful, and it's another Borg.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Pattern Buffer Preservation

Saffgor: Quietly among the best Black cards in the set, as a Think Twice with selection that resets a body to hand is nothing to scoff at. Black doesn't get a ton of self-bounce, and between this and Dark Matter Manipulator/Stitcher's Supplier you can get stuff in the yard quite fast.

BPhillipYork: This is solid card draw / selection that can be used twice. Though black now has the 3 mana, draw 2, and your opponents lose life, which is probably just stronger than this, unless you want things in your yard to reanimate them.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Salt Vampire

Saffgor: I mean, sure this seems fine enough for UB midrange in Standard. Not exciting but I won't sneeze at a mini-Thought-Knot Seer.

BPhillipYork: This episode terrified me as a 6 year old. In Magic, in the TYOOL 2026, it's not very scary. At least in Commander, in other formats its probably solid.

Commander

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Borg Incursion

Saffgor: This compares to Earthbend for its archetype of Artifact Creatures, and to that end it's alright. Used offensively it can make you unblockable, used defensively it buffers an attack, it's...alright. No indestructible is my worry, there.

BPhillipYork: That's really solid way of making more Borg, and then making your Borg unblockable, or protecting them from a non-destroying board wipe, which, okay, are the most uncommon and least good board wipes. So it's mostly just to swing through, which is still good.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Emergency Regeneration

Saffgor: Speaking of Indestructible, hey there mini-Heroic Intervention! In decks where this is better than something like a Faith's Reward, it's going to feel quite good, but White has plenty of ways to avoid a board wipe.

BPhillipYork: This is another protect your Borg army, or whatever artifact army card.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Ezri Dax, Newly Joined

Saffgor: The first White clone, and wow, it's a good one. This provides infinite sacrifice fodder alongside a Sun Titan effect—of which there are many—and more than that just helps you preserve hatebear effects after they're answered. Kill my Drannith Magistrate? Now Dax is Drannith Magistrate. I don't want to be the guy who goes 'this goes in every White deck' but it goes in a lot of White decks, trust me.

BPhillipYork: This is nice, kind of weird, and a neat way of representing the whole Trill thing. It's a reactive clone though, so it's sort of a weird thing, where you need to know you creature will die and then you're holding up mana to react, which seems like a lot of moving steps.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Merciful Mandate

Saffgor: Mass untap that's also a Fog? Sure, yeah this has applications. In any list where To Arms! makes sense, this also gets a slot.

BPhillipYork: This is a neat Fog. Weird in the way that white has of occasionally having peaceful sorts of interaction. Maybe just use it to untap all your Myr and tap them for mana again, I dunno.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Stratagem Emulator

Saffgor: Cool payoff to powering up your Artifact Creatures, but not terribly exciting.

BPhillipYork: I feel like this is only okay because the Borg were really made a little bit weaker than they should be. Even the Star Trek T:NG card game had Borg that were X/X where X = the number of Borg, and all these Borg are kind of anemic.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Type-03 Borg Vessel

Saffgor: This just seems like a slam dunk for decks already considering Foundry Inspector, and the fact literally all your spells come with a 1/1 after it's Stationed is strong. Any spell. 4 mana isn't exactly where you want to be, in terms of a discount piece/functional ramp, but that payoff isn't nothing.

BPhillipYork: This is decent enough for Borg decks. I can see it being run a lot just for artifact cost reduction, which hasn't been in white, though plenty of colorless. There are ways to fetch Spacecraft, at least a couple now, so it's tutorable in multiple ways, also creating 1/1 artifact creature tokens is nothing to sneeze at.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

U.S.S. Enterprise-E, Sovereign

Saffgor: Flickerable board wipe. If that has appeal, congrats, but I think 'board wipe typal' isn't something I'm especially keen on.

BPhillipYork: It makes me irrationally angry that this can just fight the Borg ship 1v1 and win. Like, yes, okay, in the movie under Picard's leadership the fleet targeted some special weak point on the Borg cube and it blew up, but that's because all the ships targeted it, not just the Enterprise, and the fight had been going on some time... oh well. It's a neat board wipe.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Ambulatory Reactor

Saffgor: Grand Architect-ish, but given it's a tap ability that gets granted rather than tapping the actual Creature, Haste becomes necessary to many combos. On top of that, Grand Architect is 2 mana produced, not just 1, and arrives with a board buff, and costs 1 less. Maybe Grand Architect is just better guys, I don't know.

BPhillipYork: Nice to see some Borg that aren't humans. I mean, I know Star Trek did a decent job of retconning in the end of season 5 or so why all aliens in the galaxy were basically humans (wearing masks [focused on a single human emotion]) still neat to see it on the art.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Chief Miles O'Brien

Saffgor: Wild ass line of text to attach to this trigger, and as such it seems pretty good. Great way to get out of hand with all manner of Artifacts, including a number of extra turn combos.

BPhillipYork: You can definitely abuse this with certain artifacts or creatures, though if you are consistently drawing 2 cards on multiple players turns you should probably be doing something more interesting than putting counters on things.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Data, Exploring Humanity

Saffgor: A bit expensive at 5 mana (I know I extolled the Bounty earlier, but trust me), unless you have a way to trigger this the turn it comes down. This Data loves reflexive card draw triggers, like all the old 'draw a card next upkeep' cantrip effects, and can chain those together with relative ease in a high enough density, or with a draw doubler. Cooler than he looks!

BPhillipYork: This is a pretty strong, riffling through your deck casting stuff that casts 4 or less should be pretty good. So good, given how easy it is to have a Faerie Mastermind or something like that and maybe another trigger like a Ledger Shredder that it will let you basically blow our your deck.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Optimization Annex

Saffgor: Cheap body, good effect, not much else to say. In Charge counter decks, this is a shoo-in.

BPhillipYork: This is weirdly good for all kinds of Spacecraft decks, and probably not as useful for Borg. I guess you could be like assimilating all the ships or something, as a theme.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Seven of Nine, Tertiary Adjunct

Saffgor: I much prefer this iteration of Seven, and that tap ability is well worth trying to twiddle her for; you can take infinite turns, fuel up a Darksteel Reactor, or other nefarious activities, all while filtering through your deck.

BPhillipYork: Solid way to power up your spaceships and do card selection.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Temporal Tribulation

Saffgor: This being 'permanents' is quite strong, and assures you get at worst 2 Landfall triggers. Sure, the return is slow, but in something like Princess Yue it's a slam dunk.

BPhillipYork: This is fine, kind of weird it has flashback and not beam me up, in the Star Trek set, but oh well.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Transwarp Hub

Saffgor: Awesome thing to flicker, and Stationing it up is pretty easy, so you don't mind if the Charge counters fall off.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Tuvok, Chief Tactical Officer

Saffgor: Deeply funny mechanism by which you can control combat, but calling this effect 'good' is generous. It's a fun gotcha, but not strong.

BPhillipYork: Stuff like this is kind of mean, lets you force a swing somewhere someone didn't want it, and with combat tricks can lead to multiple things dying, but also makes you unpopular. But other than the surprise, it doesn't seem that good.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Voq, Torchbearer

Saffgor: It's a hair more expensive than Activated Sleeper, but can become something that didn't die this turn. Fair trade off, and a great new color for true Body Double effects.

BPhillipYork: This is another copy a graveyard card, which is fine, Klingon whatever, haven't seen a lot of support for any kind of Klingon deck, which is kind of sad.

Next Time: The Set’s Red & Green Cards

That wraps up our look at the White, Blue, and Black cards of Star Trek. We’ll be back later this week to wrap our review up with the remaining cards.

title: James Bond Should Be a Wolf
content:
I don’t actually know what the Robert Pattinson James Bond era is going to look like; no one does yet. The Pattinson era is about 24 hours old. What we know for sure is that he has the job, and at least for the first film, Denis Villeneuve (Sicario, Dune, you know who he is) will be directing him. There is word floating around that Pattinson has a three-film deal; that’s about as officially confirmed as the murky stories around the casting itself, where all that’s really known is everything came together very quickly at the last moment. The inference you can take from that is, perhaps, that the slightly-younger men known to have auditioned for the role -- Jack Lowden, recently of an ever-growing number of seasons of Slow Horses; Josh O’Connor, recently of a number of award-winning pictures and, additionally, the third Knives Out; Callum Turner, recently married to Dua Lipa -- didn’t exactly impress the new Bond management team over at Amazon MGM Studios. It’s also possible that when Pattinson became available and sent in his tape, it simply became undeniable to put the A-lister currently on an incredible heater into the role. Pattinson’s lucky they weren’t doing this last year, which was mostly defined for him by extremely mixed reactions to Mickey 17 and Die My Love.

Alright before we go any further, though, this is going to bother me -- here’s the promotional picture for Pattinson as Bond, the one that got released alongside the news.

Robert Pattinson as James Bond. Credit: Jaap Buitendijk/Amazon MGM Studios

I am not what you would call a “gun guy.” I don’t know the things, and outside of fiction, I don’t particularly like the things. But I’ve learned enough about them to play characters in tabletop RPGs that seem like they know what they’re talking about in genre work like Hunter: The Reckoning or Delta Green, which means I know enough to say that the thing on the top of this gun is a reflex sight, and the thing below it is some kind of tactical flashlight, and aesthetically speaking: What in the world is James Bond doing with that shit on his gun? Get that outta here. That’s Call of Duty multiplayer behavior. Hopefully they just had it hanging around for the shoot and the new team’s concept of James Bond isn’t a guy who needs to upgrade his pistol to add a bar of accuracy at the cost of a bar of handling.

GoldenEye 007 for the Nintendo 64 aside, the character isn’t iconic for his gunplay; the Bond game out earlier in the year understood that. IOI’s vision of Bond didn’t quite do it for me either, though; a bit too modern, and a bit too nice. In the cutscenes, that is -- in the gameplay he was pretty much right there. My ideal Bond doesn’t do much aiming down sights; honestly, if he’s shooting people, I’d prefer him looking them in the eyes while he does it from close range, maybe after hitting them a couple times with the gun. And while you’re at it, hopefully he’s doing it somewhere between the years 1956 and 1988. That’s a range for period pieces that covers a couple different actual periods, but all of them are years where the character’s image (both his self-image and the one he has as a brand) as the ultimate man of the empire for post-war Great Britain makes the most sense. I enjoyed the post-Cold War malaise of the first 90s Bond offering, speaking of GoldenEye, but the Brosnan films managed to land that once before becoming completely unmoored in their search for suitable new villains in the post-Soviet era. And, let’s be honest, Great Britain: You’re not what you once were, either. You don’t want to see James Bond up there on the screen representing the empire and the enterprise of Keir Starmer and Nigel Farage anymore than we do. At least for us, that’d be conceptually funny. But Bond is a retreat into the past; the IOI game attempted to bring the franchise into the present with a story about evil tech CEOs and AI that felt credible as a video game plot but was merely acceptable and unremarkable as far as a Bond story goes. It didn’t help that they handed Lenny Kravitz the only actual role that jumped off the screen the way bad guys in Bond movies used to, because Kravitz did not have the juice for it. Unless Villeneuve has an idea to completely remake the franchise -- which is presumably not what he was hired to do and not what Amazon MGM is paying for, but is at least theoretically on the table -- the next James Bond film has the choice of either continuing to pretend the end of the 20th century didn’t actually happen, and Great Britain is still as it once was, or it can just actually go back there to when the suit still fit.

And in that spirit, I want the proper James Bond for the era: James Bond as the wolf. This is not quite the same as Daniel Craig’s Bond, who was the sociopathic thug humanized, over and over again, by the love of a good woman -- about three-fourths of Craig’s Casino Royale and bits and pieces of Quantum of Solace had the sort of energy I was looking for, but especially in the later entries (as Craig himself checked out of the franchise mentally) there were only echoes of that character remaining as the aristo Spy Batman lore of Skyfall and all the Blofeld nonsense of Spectre took the character over. Thanks to a quirk of when I saw the movies for the first time growing up and what I was reading when I did, the character in literature I identify the most with what I want out of Bond predates him -- Philip Lombard, the second-to-last to die in Agatha Christie’s And Then There Were None. He is, in fact, described consistently in terms of animalistic predation; Christie uses the panther as her first touchpoint, because at the time the novel takes place the imagination of British Empire was captured in no small part by Africa, but on at least two occasions his “wolflike smile” is mentioned, and that’s the detail that stuck with me -- it’s the detail Vera mentions in the last moments the two share together. Lombard is distinguished by being a genuinely brave, accomplished, skilled, and charismatic man; this sits alongside his self-interest, propensity for violence, and misogyny, the last of which is his downfall as he doesn’t believe Vera, a woman, has the mettle to kill him. These are all distinguishing qualities of Bond to me, even -- especially! -- those three negative traits; I see some of them in Connery, in Dalton, definitely in Craig, and I am very confident that Pattinson can bring that same energy to the character, especially with Denis Villeneuve directing. Obviously there can be quite a light touch on the misogyny unless the Bond girl is going to do him like Vera did Lombard (it's a brave new world, anything is technically possible under new management), but the first scenes between Craig's Bond and Vesper Lynd don't work like they do without the chauvinism of empire informing him.

But let’s be real: Robert Pattinson can bring any energy he wants to the character. They could tell him the next film’s going to be a love letter to the Roger Moore days, and what’s more an intentional comedy to boot, and he’d deliver a fantastic farce of a Bond performance. The film would bomb, but Pattinson would be impeccable in it. So he’ll do fine in whatever Villeneuve and the new Bond executive management team are cooking up for him -- I am ambivalent on whether or not this new group will step in it, because we haven’t seen what they are or are not capable of yet.

https://bsky.app/profile/danielduncan.bsky.social/post/3n2gua5zgds2g

That’s not a confidence I had about the other named public choices. O’Connor is one thing -- he hasn’t proven he can play this exact kind of role yet, maybe, but come on; he’d probably kill it. I can see both the studio wanting a surer thing and him maybe not wanting to sign a four movie deal just as he’s coming into his own as a critical darling. (In fact, as I'm putting the finishing touches on this, there's reporting coming out that O'Connor removed himself from consideration for precisely those reasons.) Callum Turner is coming off a hard L with that weird movie about the Sex Purge; not only was it a bomb but very notably, Turner’s character doesn’t actually get laid during the Sex Purge. That’s evangelical behavior, not Bond behavior. And Jack Lowden…well, earlier in the day before Pattinson was announced as Bond, it came out that Slow Horses had been renewed for an additional two seasons, so if he stays there everyone will be happy. He is very good at doing River Cartwright things. Not a single one of those things ever made me think he’d be any good at James Bond. If there’s a movie spy role he fits into for me, it’s not even in the Bond franchise; he reminds me of nobody so much as William Brandt, Jeremy Renner’s secret agent character from the Mission: Impossible series of films. This isn’t me being mean! If I was being mean I’d say he reminds me of Josh Holloway’s character from the Mission: Impossible series, who dies in the Ghost Protocol cold open. If Lowden had to be a Bond, he'd be the James Bond from the IOI video game, not the one you'd see on the silver screen. (There was a report that Nicholas Hoult was under consideration? Not a Bond for me, but a fantastic choice for when they do the 006 MI6-agent-turned-supervillain thing again.)

title: The 5 most undervalued cards in MTG Star Trek
content:
Judging card values before a new Magic: The Gathering set has actually been released is a mug's game. The shiny spells are buoyed up by hype and by the time the wrappers are ripped and that new card smell has worn off, most of them will be far cheaper than predicted.

Not always though. There are always a few outlier cards that are actually undervalued, and these show their stuff and spike as soon as players get to try them out. That's particularly true for MTG Star Trek, because Worlds, the biggest tournament of the year, kicked off on release day, immediately putting the new cards to the test in the crucible of high-level competitive play.

Below, you'll find five cards that have spiked in price over the few days since Star Trek prerelease.

The Naked Time

Price at prerelease:$0.50

Price now: $2.90

An uncommon that's making a storm in Standard, this card performed well in the most popular deck at Worlds (Boros Pixie) and some people were even wondering if it could be banned (turns out it's not even the greatest uncommon in MTG Star Trek). The Naked Time is a powerful card, giving a creature a boost and haste while ramping you in red. Honestly, it's playable even in decks that aren't looking to bounce it before the third time counter gets placed.

Deep Space 9

Price at prerelease: $14.50

Price now: $40

As a big mana mythic, Deep Space 9 was expected to be costly, but no one had this down as a $40 card. It's obviously fantastic in spacecraft decks like the new Captain Picard, but unlike most examples of its card type, your deck doesn't need to be all about rockets and charge counters for Deep Space 9 to be a good fit.

With the ability to grab up to four free permanents every turn, Deep Space 9 is just a brilliant nine-drop to cheat into play. It belongs in Eldrazi decks, artifact decks - basically any deck that can cast something this powerful.

Captain James T. Kirk

Price at prerelease: $6.50

Price now: $22

An efficient, aggressive creature that can grant you a lot of value when your back's against the wall, Captain James T. Kirk is a key part of the Boros deck that was so popular at Worlds, and as a result it saw a huge spike over the past week.

Jadzia Dax, Living Legacy

Price at prerelease: $7.70

Price now: $23.50

Another card that's shown its worth in Standard, Jadzia Dax is a useful ramp creature (and a beater in her own right in a long game) that's proven popular in a rising Selesnya Landfall deck. This is still a much-played archetype, appearing en masse in the recent tournament. It looks exactly like the mono-green decks that were doing the rounds a month back, only with white removal and sometimes main-decking Doorkeeper Thrull to shut off everyone else's triggers.

Jadzia variants have a +1/+1 counter subtheme, using the broken Strixhaven spell Practiced Offense to help close out games.

Anthropological Mission

Price at prerelease: $0.50

Price now: $8

The true breakout star from Magiccon Atlanta - Stefan Schütz won Worlds with an Izzet deck that played four copies of this uncommon enchantment that no one was ready for. While most of the missions seem a little too slow, the blue one in the cycle only needs three counters before it's not looting but actually netting you a card every time you play a non-creature spell. Schütz's deck ran 30 instants and sorceries and not a single creature, and absolutely drowns in card advantage.

How are you finding the Star Trek set? Let us know over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: StarCraft Tabletop Miniatures Game: Protoss Unit Overview
content:
StarCraft Tabletop Miniatures Game brings the war for the Koprulu sector to your tabletop, letting you build, paint, and play armies of Terran, Zerg, and Protoss units as they fight toward victory. And while the game initially launched with a very limited roster, continued new releases offer new units that fill diverse roles on the tabletop, opening up novel strategies and unique playstyles to suit any aspiring general’s tastes.

Today, we’re here to look at the various non-Hero units available to every Protoss faction and how to use them on the table. If you’re looking for guidance on how to get the most out of your Protoss units, read on.

Core

Every Protoss Faction card gives you 3 Core slots, except Nerazim which only gives you 2. And given that several of the stronger faction cards (including the Nexus and Warp Prism) tack on a few more, you’re likely to find yourself spending at least 5 supply on Core choices.

Thankfully, both of the Core options currently available to Protoss are pretty good: Zealots are a workhorse close range damage-dealer that provides a reasonably durable 2-supply unit suitable for scrapping over objectives, while Adepts combine respectable shooting output with best-in-class mobility and utility tricks.

Zealots

Zealots can only attack in melee, but that’s fine. If they can make contact, Zealots hit pretty damn hard: out of the box, they’ll roll 9 Impact dice on the charge, then follow that up with 12 more attacks in the combat phase. And they’re reasonably tough, too, having 3 shields and 4 HP per unit. That means that killing even a single Zealot requires 7 damage, which is enough damage to rip a big, bloody chunk out of nearly any other Core option.

Zealots are the Core unit in the game that keeps efficiency uninhibited for the most amount of damage, only dropping their first model after taking the 7th point of damage. Protoss players should take advantage of this by positioning Zealots within the control range of mission markers they expect to be contested, or at least able to declare a charge onto any enemy unit that comes within control range. It takes a real damage commitment to threaten Zealots, so we want to use Zealots to force the enemy damage dealers into positions where we can counter-attack and remove them. Sometimes a few Zealots must be sacrificed to win the battle at hand. Their lives are for Aiur after all!

Zealots need Leg Enhancements. The extra damage provided by My Life For Aiur! or the extra durability provided by Zealous Round don’t matter if the unit is not in the correct position, and while at first glance this ability appears to be a 2" move, that actually becomes a 5" stretch thanks to StarCraft TMG’s coherency rules. Don’t bother with We Stand As One, it is the worst of their upgrades as it incentivizes you to group your Zealots up in melee. We have too few units for that. If you have twenty points buy My Life and Zealous Round instead.

Zealots have Speed 4/7, which leaves them 13" away from the Marines. But with Leg Enhancements, the extra 2" move works out to another 5", leaving them within 8" and not only able to charge, but likely to make it.

Would you pay 1 Psionic Energy out of the 7 to 8 you have access to on a turn to have Zealots go from unable to charge anything to 66% of the time they charge their target? I know I would.

Adepts

Adepts are a ranged combat unit with powerful utility. Their shooting isn’t bad: 8 dice for the unit with a d3+1 surge against light is a decent statline. And while their shorter 8” range puts them at risk of being charged, at 3HP with 2 shields, they’re reasonably tough and their Glaive Cannons are better than you’d expect in engagement thanks to Anti-Evade (1).

Psionic Transfer is their standout ability, and it offers the unit absolutely incredible flexibility. Some of the uses are obvious: you can use it to leapfrog a unit up the board to get into position to stand on an objective, or stick it out to give your entire army Precision (1) against a key enemy unit. But the extreme mobility combined with the fact that you don’t need line of sight to place it can open up some really useful options, giving you a decent skirmisher unit that’s near impossible to nail down.

Adepts are your errand-runners. One good combo is to Deploy the Adepts their full speed plus coherency toward an objective within 19” of your entry edge, and then send their Psionic Transfer Shade toward a different objective. In the Assault Phase you can Run with the Adepts and get close enough to Sticky Control of that Mission Marker before teleporting to the Shade.

Protoss Adepts use their Shade to outplay a Terran Siege Tank.

There's a lot going on here, so let's break it down: The Adepts aim for an objective within 19" of their Entry Edge.  In this case they would like to sticky the blue objective and not get shot by the perfidious enemy Siege Tank, then end on the red objective also not able to be shot at next round unless somebody moves. For most units, this is impossible. For Adepts? It's just another day at the office.

They first move 5" plus a 3" stretch, ending outside of 18" of the enemy Tank (move A). Here they spend 1 PE to throw a Psionic Shade to the red objective on their left, which they will teleport to at the end of the round. After the Siege Tank has activated in the Assault Phase, the Adepts can Run for another 8" total which puts them within the 3" control radius of the blue objective (move B). The End of Round Scoring check happens first, and the blue objective becomes "sticky" controlled by our Adepts. Then End of Round Effects occur and the Adepts make their final move to safety (move C). They end within coherency of the shade but not overlapping its base and all within 1" of a wall that will provide them Direct Cover of incoming Terran fire next turn, allowing them to avoid enemy attacks even if the wall isn't tall enough to provide Full Cover.

On top of their outstanding utility, Adepts are also deceptively solid against melee enemies. Unwary foes may try to charge them early and often, but they’re better at standing their ground than you might expect. First, at 2 HP per model with 3 points of shields, your opponent will need to deal at least 5 points of damage to remove a model, giving them a decent chance to absorb any Impact hits on the charge without losing effectiveness. And once they weather that damage, their Glaive Cannons’ Anti-Evade (1) and anti-light surge lets them clap back that much harder.

Upgrade-wise, if you’ve got the points there’s a case to be made for any of them. Resonating Glaives is probably the standout, allowing 4 of these to shoot with slightly more effectiveness than 6 unstimmed Marines, though it does cost 1 PE. Guidance is cheaper and pushes their ranged weapon to Anti-Evade (2), making them more reliable ranged threats both in engagement and against any enemy that can get an on-demand Evade. Glaive Strike is the most situational, upgrading their melee attack to gain both d3 surge and Pierce (2) against Light targets. But if you’re expecting them to eat a lot of charges, both of those rules are great ways to help make sure they acquit themselves well once they get touched.

Elite

Elite slots are, somewhat unsurprisingly, a bit harder to come by than Core, though you’ll have no trouble finding room for plenty of them if you really want a walker-heavy force. Both Protoss Elite options sport the “Armoured” tag and pack weaponry designed to demonstrate their superiority over anything else with it. You’ll generally want at least a couple of these units to deal with any enemy armor, but the specific choice will depend on whether you’d rather combine that anti-armor firepower with impressive mobility or best-in-class durability.

Stalkers

These spindly walkers were Protoss’s only unit with a surge against armoured until the release of the Immortal, and they still find use in that role thanks their Particle Disruptors’ decent shotcount, d3 surge, and flat 2 damage characteristic. And between their 4+ save, 6 HP, and 3 shields, they’re tough enough that taking them down will usually require your opponent to actually try. They’re worth considering including in your list even if only as a reasonably-priced option to deal with armored enemies your other units can struggle to handle.

But the biggest thing Stalkers have going for them is their speed: these guys are fast. If you’re willing to burn 2 PE for Blink and the Warp Prism’s Phase, a pair of Stalkers can move a staggering 25” in a single phase, including 2 Place effects that will allow you to move clear through blocking terrain if needed. Between that and their 12” range, a pair of Stalkers is almost never going to find themselves out of range of whatever unit you want to point them at, allowing them to serve as a potent rapid-reaction force that can exert supply over an objective in one corner of the board one round, then leap clear across to the other side to make an enemy armoured unit regret its life decisions the next.

The Stalker upgrade Path of Shadows is the stand-out of the two upgrades, as gaining Hidden until the next action is performed allows them to force the enemy to either commit a Tactical Card to reveal them or otherwise move units within 4” where the Stalkers still get an Evade for their enemy trouble. Because it can be used in any phase, it also forces enemy shooting to contend with the possibility that the Stalkers will shoot first and then hide after. The other upgrade, Fury of the Nerazim, is for Stalkers that activate after their enemies in the Assault phase, and gives them Instant to thwart enemy defensive Reactions. This upgrade synergizes with Path of Shadows as being successfully Hidden in the Movement Phase means Stalkers can wait to shoot until their key enemy target has acted in the Assault Phase. Fury of the Nerazim is still really good when you can use it, but you'll usually look to Path of Shadows first, if only because it's a lot easier to get mileage out of Fury when your unit can benefit from hidden to wait out enemy attacks.

One final thing to keep in mind is that you don’t have to take a pair of Stalkers. It’s not always going to be an optimal play since one model costs nearly 2/3 of the pair rather than half and adding an activation can mean ceding the initiative in the Assault phase, but there are some upsides worth considering here. First, the unit gets 3 shields regardless of its size, so that single model has 9 effective HP. And if you take 2 of them rather than 1, each of them gets a surge die when they attack. Finally, if you’ve got a single Elite slot you want to fill, a singleton Stalker is currently the only way to do it. At current points costs, you’ll frequently find that it’s not worth it, but it is the cheapest non-Hero way to add some anti-armored punch to your list.

Immortals

An Immortal is not only likely the single toughest unit in the game right now, it also packs some serious heat on offense. Its stock weapons, Photon Disruptors, hit like trucks, and will absolutely tear through armored targets since their dice are split between two profiles, each of which gets a surge die. And if they’re not powerful enough for you, each can be upgraded to a Phase Disruptor, which trade away the Long Range (16”) rule to deal 3 damage against armoured units and get rid of the base weapons’ Concentrated Fire (1). This makes the unit even deadlier into nearly all targets, and it’s often worth swapping out at least one.

The use-case here is very straightforward: put one in the middle of the table and force your opponent to deal with it. Between Improved Barrier and Shield Overcharge, you’ve got two very powerful defensive abilities right there on the sheet, and it’s a great target for defensive buffs from Tactical cards.

Speaking of Tactical cards, Warp Prism is an excellent card to help you get every drop of utility out of the Immortal. Use it in the early game to get the Immortal onto the table in a forward position so it can step out and immediately start contesting objectives and ruining enemy armor’s day. But it really comes into its own later in the game, when Phase allows you to blink the thing out of engagement, then move 7”. Used late in the movement phase, it can let you avoid the engagement penalty for falling back and prevent enemies from taking Evade rolls against it. Using it like this might not be as obnoxious as solid Warp Prism/Immortal micro in the PC game can, but it’s a useful trick to keep in mind when it counts.

Protoss Immortal for StarCraft: the Miniatures Game | Credit: Blizzard Entertainment/Archon Studios

Most of the upgrades on Immortals are worth considering. For the Ancients is the standout, giving you Precision (1) against targets more than 8” away. Thanks to the many movement tricks available to Protoss, maintaining that minimum range against whatever you’re trying to kill often won’t be difficult, and the rule triggers on both the unit’s guns, making it more potent than you might expect. And as we mentioned before, swapping out at least one of the guns for Phase Disruptors is often worth a look, as it’ll make your Immortal better at dealing with basically any unit that isn’t a Hero. Finally, if you’ve got the points, Shield Overcharge is worth a look, especially if you’re worried about being overwhelmed with lots of low-damage attacks more than taking a few high-damage ones. The final upgrade, Fury Unyielding, isn’t bad when it triggers, but it’s often too situational to be worthwhile: both the Immortal and its target have to be in range of the same objective, and there’s no lack of 20-point upgrades for Protoss units that don’t come with that sort of condition on their use.

Support

Finally, we’ve got the Support units. Sentries are the sort of defensive unit you’re probably expecting to see in a support role, offering multiple ways to boost nearby units’ durability and frustrate your opponent’s plans to engage. High Templar, on the other hand, remain true to their counterparts in the PC games as a more offensive caster archetype that can deal impressive damage to opponents that overextend and discourage them from playing aggressively.

Sentries

Sentries are your defensive support choice, offering very little in the way of offensive output but bringing a couple of nice defensive options and one of the trickiest utility tools in the game. Guardian Shield is the first defensive choice, letting you choose a friendly unit within 4” and removing a die from every ranged attack made against it this round. The effectiveness of this ability turns on a couple of factors, but taking dice out of the attack pool is incredibly powerful since it lowers the maximum amount of damage that unit can do. Plus, since the ability isn’t a Reaction, it works even if you’re targeted by an Instant attack, making it particularly great in the Protoss mirror. The other defensive option is Restoration, which lets you clear all the debuffs off of a unit as a reaction to your opponent applying a new one. Functioning as a “counter” to the buff you really care about is good enough, but flushing off any others you’ve managed to accumulate is solid as well. And while there currently aren’t that many Debuffs you’ll have to worry about, this ability will likely really come into its own once Stukov and his ability to apply the Infested status to your units makes it out into the wild.

Generally, Guardian Shield and Restoration (as well as the Hallucination upgrade, which we’ll discuss below) define the Sentry’s role as a support unit that follows a handful of units around and makes them that much harder to remove. Having a unit of Sentries follow some Zealots around is a solid use-case that will help make sure that melee unit gets into position to do what you brought it for, but just about any unit will appreciate the extra durability they bring. And while Sentries aren’t that tough on their own, any attack your opponent sends against them is an attack they’re not putting into a real damage-dealer, so losing them is often fine if it means a more dangerous unit gets where it’s going unscathed.

Force Fields are an incredibly powerful trick, letting you corral your opponent’s key units by keeping them away from objectives and vulnerable units. An important thing to keep in mind is that Force Fields aren’t terrain, which has pros and cons. The major downside is that you can’t use them to block line of sight, but in exchange units like Raptors who ignore terrain still have to find a way around them. A well-placed force field can absolutely ruin your opponent’s day and change the momentum of the battle round. Played wisely, you can split your opponent’s force in two, protect vulnerable units from charges, and just generally be a tremendous pain in the neck, all for the reasonable cost of 1 PE.

Because the Sentries and Force Field are each less than 1" from each other and the nearby walls, the Marines can't walk past them.

Unfortunately, while a single force field is usually enough to stop bigger units like Siege Tanks, Queens, and Immortals from going wherever they want, the gap clearance rules make it harder to lock down anything size 2 or smaller. Thankfully, there are two ways to get around this: the obvious one is the Solid-Field Projectors upgrade, which lets your unit drop a second Force Field, though you’ll still have to pay for both. But there’s another, free option: use the Sentries to bodyblock. You can set them up just under 1” apart from each other, then drop a Force Field just under 1” from one of them. Line them up properly, and you can plug a gap of up to 10.5”, so long as they can stay alive. This won’t work as well if there are ranged enemies nearby who can shoot them off the table so another threat can run or charge through, but it’s a solid option that can slow your opponent down in a pinch.

Upgrades-wise, Hallucination is the go-to choice. It’s a 0 PE reaction that allows a unit within 4” to make an Evade roll against a ranged attack. It’s not quite as powerful as the High Templar Farsight upgrade, and we’ll discuss the differences in more detail below, but it’s still worth taking as another way to keep a key unit alive.

High Templar

On the other hand, High Templar serve as an offensive spellcaster that punishes opponents for poor positioning. Un-upgraded, they’re fine, if a little unimpressive. They’ve got a ranged attack that’s a little better than a Sentry’s (if only because it has a surge value), and their core ability, Feedback, means that enemy Psionic or Mechanized units that rely on Special Abilities have to be judicious about using them or they’ll take a pile of nonlethal damage, leaving them at risk of dying to a stiff breeze.

But if you’re asking how to use them, Psionic Storm is what you’re probably here for. It’s pricey at 2 PE, but you can use it to really mess with your opponent’s game plan. Hold your unit’s activation until later in the round and you can all but guarantee both a chunk of damage on a key unit and force your opponent to decide if they really want to keep standing in that particular spot. You can also preemptively cast it near objectives or choke points to discourage your opponent from sending units to contest them, potentially leaving you free to move in with impunity. And if an enemy unit is in your storm at the end of the Movement phase, you can charge it to force it to take more damage at the end of the Assault phase, though doing so will probably result in the charging unit catching some strays. Just keep in mind that Protoss are currently the only army without a 2-resource Tactical card, meaning that you’ll have to either flip two cards to cast this, or find a way to reduce the cost.

But don’t sleep on Farsight: it lets you choose a unit within 12” to be allowed to make an Evade roll against any number of attacks this round. This functions like a more powerful version of the Sentries’ Hallucination, letting you use it from further away and potentially providing a benefit more than once per round, but it does have two notable downsides. First, it costs 1 PE, meaning you’ll have to spend a resource to get the benefit. Given the magnitude of the effect, that’s probably fine, but keep it in mind. The other downside is the more interesting one: you have to use it in the Movement phase, not as a reaction to your opponent’s shooting. Forcing you to use it on the front end means that your opponent knows for certain whether the rule is in play, potentially informing which units they choose to attack. This isn’t necessarily always going to be a bad thing–if there’s only one unit available for them to attack then you know where to put this–but the closer and scrappier the game is, the more important it’ll be to make sure you get this right. By contrast, Hallucination is more limited both in range and number of uses, but the fact that it’s a reaction means you have some certainty that it’ll matter when you need it to.

The choice of upgrades also impacts how large of a unit you’ll want: if you take the larger, 4-model unit, it gets a 1 PE discount on its first Special Ability each round and adds 1 to the rolls to see how much damage its Psionic Storm deals. This is obviously worth considering for a unit you’re planning to cast Storm with, since every time it does so it’ll be both cheaper and more effective. But Farsight? At 1 PE, there are plenty of other ways to bring the cost down to 0, and you might be fine with hard-casting it in a pinch. Smaller units of High Templar can also afford to play a little more aggressively to make use of feedback, since they’re only 130 points. If you’re looking at High Templar primarily as a vector for getting Evade rolls on your Zealots and Adepts, consider whether you can get away with saving 70 points by only bringing 2.

Final Thoughts

Protoss units are strong, tough, and tricky, frequently requiring smart play and finesse to get the most out of them. But if you’ve got a good sense of how your units work and what their highest and best use is, you can absolutely tear through hordes of enemy units and leave them wondering whether being outnumbered was actually better for you.

In a 2000 point list, you’ll almost certainly want to bring an Immortal to serve as a durable central objective holder. It’ll also double as a way to deal with enemy armor, and you can add a little more punch to that side of things by bringing some Stalkers. Those Stalkers, in turn, combine with a couple cheap units of Adepts to give you plenty of movement tricks that will help you flexibly adapt to your enemy’s gameplan. And when it comes time to really get into a scrap over a contested objective, send in the Zealots to slice your foes to ribbons. Backstop all of this with some support units to taste, and Protoss units offer a solid foundation to build on, even if they’re a bit tricky to get the most value out of.
