title: Will Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War IV escape the GTA VI tsunami?
content:
Grand Theft Auto VI is so hotly anticipated, so hyped, so pre-emptively popular, that many videogame publishers shifted the release date of their biggest titles to arrive at least a month ahead of it, or pushed back into the next year. Warhammr 40,000: Dawn of War IV isn't one of them: set to release on December 3, it's going to be well inside the GTA VI blast zone, with wallets emptied and the media cycle dominated by GTA commentary. Can it survive on its own merits?

Ordinarily, I wouldn't even ask this kind of question about two games so totally different as Dawn of War 4 and GTA 6. DoW 4 is real time strategy, GTA 6is an open world third person action game; DoW 4 is set in the grimdark Warhammer 40,000 universe, GTA 6 is set in a satirical take on contemporary Florida; DoW 4 has a pulp war story, GTA 6 has a bonnie-and-clyde tale of criminals in love; DoW 4 is a PC-first title, GTA 6 is at home on consoles.

But according to consumer data website Sensor Tower, GTA 6 has sold just short of 15 million units, for a revenue of $1.45 billion, on XBox and Playstation alone, and it's not even out yet. Those numbers are unfathomable; between the release of the original Dawn of War in September 2004 and Sega acquiring the franchise in January 2013, DoW 1 and DoW 2 managed combined sales of a comparatively paltry 7 million.

DoW 4 is a glossy RTS, and it's trading on a great brand and a lot of nostalgic fondness. The original DoW was both an innovative game in its genre, and the best Warhammer 40k game for decades either side of its release; in marketing and interviews, the developers have been clear that the original DoW was a guiding light for the new title. That's a good strategy for gathering in the flock of millennials who grew up playing Dawn of War, or RTS gamers pining for the good old days of the early '00s, who are now playing other titles.

The issue is that - as video essayist Static Canvas lays out in the video below - GTA VI's nostalgic pulling power (not to mention marketing and general hype) is off the chart. This is the kind of cultural event that convinces people who haven't touched a videogame in a decade to pick up a games consoles. The GTA pull is going to be felt all the way throughout the gaming community.

A lot depends on what DoW 4 needs to be considered 'successful'. The original DoW was released when the RTS was a mainstream PC gaming genre and the premier format for online multiplayer strategy. RTS games have shrunk in prominence since then, but the gaming audience as a whole has grown. Does publisher Deep Silver expect DoW 4 to capture the hardcore RTS market, the wider strategy market, or to reach out and pluck strategy-curious fans from further afield?

A lower sales target is easier to reach, obviously, but fans of a niche genre should also be less affected by the allure of GTA. Strategy games reward gaming monogamy by providing a more engaging experience to more engaged players. That's an audience less likely to be drawn in by games outside their wheelhouse. Just as importantly, strategy streamers and gaming websites are way less likely to change their coverage, compared to generalists.

But if DoW 4 needs to sell like a blockbuster, and publisher Deep Silver expects that to happen in the release window, that could be a problem. It will have to reach beyond the core strategy game audience, to people who play a variety of games. And to make blockbuster numbers, it will need to tap into a specific kind of customer - the "one game per year gamer", or OGPYG.

The archetype for the OGPYG is someone who pre-orders the annual Call of Duty or Madden NFL update every year, but otherwise isn't interested in shopping for games. They could just as easily be a Switch owner who only buys first party Nintendo titles, or a grand strategy player who buys every Hearts of Iron expansion religiously. They trust big, well-marketed games to offer high quality experiences, and their buying decisions are as much determined by how they spend their time as what titles cost. This is the kind of customer who will pay an extra $35 to get a premium pre-order, but would never spend that on an indie title.

Many OGPYGs simply won't consider strategy titles at all. But DoW 4 might appeal to some - it's got the Warhammer 40k label, the quality DoW brand, and it's a very highly produced game. But if we look further ahead, at a title currently set to release in 2027, is suddenly seems a lot more missable - Total War: Warhammer 40,000 is on the horizons.

If you're a core strategy gamer, the differences between the two titles are obvious; RTS and Grand Strategy are not the same kind of game. But from the perspective of someone who makes very infrequent game purchases, the promise that Total War: Warhammer 40k will arrive some time in the next 12 months could make it a lot easier to drop DoW 4 and pick up GTA 6 instead.

If DoW 4 does suffer from poor launch day sales, that may not spell the end. Continuous economic depressions in the West, and the drought of components for gaming PCs, mean gamers are increasingly buying older and cheaper games, which digital distribution keeps permanently available. A game with a weak launch week can recover and have good lifetime sales, something that used to be impossible. Strategy games are well placed to take advantage of this, particularly through the sale of multiple small DLC.

DoW 4 looks like a strong entry in the underserved RTS genre, and I expect the core audience for strategy games will be less easily drawn away by a mainstream blockbuster. Publisher Deep Silver has a track record of supporting (at least some of) its games over the long term. But I don't envy the developers at King Art Games launching this ship into warp storm Grand Theft Auto.

What do you think? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: [40K] Weekend Update: November 16, 2026
content:
In our Weekend Update series, we cover the big events and stories that are happening each week in wargames, so you can stay updated and informed every week.

Another week another update, with more events around the country and some which were undoubtedly upended or affected by the widespread FAA grounding of flights on Friday afternoon. Pour one out for anyone who couldn't make it to their event or hasn't made it home yet.

Let’s dive into the weekend's big events.

Clement Tournade Upsets at Kempton Park with Aeldari

The biggest singles GT of the weekend was Games Workshop's National Tournament Series event in Kempton Park, a 121 player event with five rounds of play. Clement Tournade surprised everyone by winning the event with Aeldari (a faction which has struggled so far in 11th edition). Tournade's build employs a combination of the Seer Council and Armoured Warhost Detachments and its highlights include two Storm Guardian bricks with five attached Psykers which can take advantage of the stratagems in Seer Council. These are supported by a 10-man Fire Dragon unit with Fuegan and rounded out by the Avatar of Khaine and Jain Zar. They're supported by a ton of cheap trash, which helps the list run Priority Assets as its primary mission. It's a great place to start if you're looking for inspiration on how to play Aeldari in the new meta.

Playing Priority Assets support by a ton of cheap trash this list like a great place to start if you are an Aeldari playing looking for guidance in the new meta.

Also undefeated at the event were Malik Amin Rubio (Adeptus Mechanicus), Clement - Immortus Riu (Astra Militarum), and Tom Godfrey (Orks), who finished with an astonishing 500 battle points over five rounds. Stay tuned for more on their lists in Competitive Innovations this week.

Matt Evans Wins Springs Thundercluckers with Tyranids

Thundercluckers was comparatively a smaller event - just 61 players - with five rounds of play. Matt Evans won the event with a Tyranids Invasion Fleet list that's just sporting a very cool brew. Playing Invasion Fleet in Priority Assets he was able to eat the completion with a surprisingly large amount of Tyrant Guard and Warriors. Rounded out of a ton of Gaunts, some support pieces, and a Tyranofex, this list really has a unique build when compared to the more popular Norn spam. Also shout out to Trae Burnett for also finishing 5-0 with a Take and Hold CSM build sport Veterans of the Long War and Cabal of Chaos.

Brad Chester Wins Da Boyz GT

The weekend's mandatory Marines winner, Brad Chester won the five round, 59-player Da Boyz with a Take and Hold list using Assault Brethren and Stormlance with Deathwatch Support sprinkled in. Congratulations as well to Joseph Sault, who went undefeated with a Space Marines list running Deathwatch Support, Assault Brethren, and Phobos Shadow Force.

Team Spain Wins Autumn International Team Tournament 

The massive - 534 players! - International Team Tournament is the highlight teams event of the quarter for the UK, a UKTC event featuring six rounds of play. Team Spain absolutely dominated their competition at the event, scoring a huge win over team Ignite in the final round with a 67-33 victory that included blowout wins over some of the game's biggest names.

Congratulations to:

  • Alejandro Mancuso Serrano (Aeldari - TAH)
  • Borja FM (Space Wolves - PTF)
  • Falco (Death Guard - DIS)
  • Gonzalo "Raven" de La Moneda (Emperor's Children - RCN)
  • Terroxer El Rojo (Thousand Sons - PAS)

Danmarksmesterskaberne i 40K for Hold 2026 Won by Grumpy Old Bastards

The weekend's second largest teams event, this was a 240-player, five round event which took place in Denmark and had three teams finish 4-0-1, including Grumpy old bastards, Drekar, and Øst for Kasakhstan. Grumpy old bastards managed to barely squeak out a win on tiebreakers. Congrats to:

  • Martin Bræmer Nielsen
  • Michael Roune
  • Paul Bridge
  • Simon Darre
  • Thomas Donslund

Prague GT - Fall 2026 Crushed by Moravian Eagles

It was a big weekend for European teams events, and the Prague Fall GT was a 175-player, five round tournament held in Prague. The Moravian Eagles won the event with a 5-0 record and were the only undefeated team. Congrats to:

  • Antonin Man
  • Dan Sochor
  • Jan Tlustý
  • Luis Stiemerling
  • Lukáš Tölg

The NTL 8 Player Championship

The biggest teams event in the US was the NTL 8-Player Championship, a 112-player 8-man teams event taking place over five rounds. The even was the final tournament of the 2026 American Teams Championship season and took place in Cleveland, Tennessee. The top two teams each received qualifier tickets to the 2027 World Championships of Warhammer.

The mid-Atlantic-based team Nemesis won the event as the only undefeated team, going 4-0-1 with a narrow draw to ProTabletop in the final round. Congrats to:

  • Ari C
  • Dan Meloro
  • Jack Murphy
  • Jeffrey Kolodner
  • Joshua Campbell
  • Noah Keeth
  • TJ Lanigan
  • Zach Point
Marneus Calgar in the Armour of Antilochus. Credit: SRM

Space Marines Still Dominate Without Deathwatch; Custodes Finding Their Place

Turns out that Space Marines are still very good. Some events have begun to use the WCW FAQ, resulting in a general dropping of Deathwatch as an ally option, though they are still very solid. Space Wolves and Dark Angels take up the banner as the Marines of choice for the refined competitive player, while generic Marines still follows with an above 50% win rate.

Custodes are not one of top armies this week but they pulled both an above 50% win rate but also snagged two undefeated results! No event win this week but they are on pace to sang one soon and as the codex gets more fully explored I won’t be surprised if they are a faction of interest once their main predator, Space Marines, hopefully gets nerfed.

Thousand Sons and T’au left the dumps with huge win rates, but a tiny player size means this was most likely a fluke. Blood Angels, CSM, Leagues of Votann, Emperors Children, and Chaos Knights round up the bottom. A lot of these I expected but I am surprised to see Blood Angels so low after their decent results in the past few weeks. Hopefully the slate early next month can salvage some of these lower performers who have been stuck here for a long time, like Chaos Knights

40k Christmas Battleforces Up for Preorder  

At a retail value of $255 dollars the new Christmas battleforces are live and ready to purchase. As expected the CSM box sold out within the first few minutes - turns out Defilers are really hard to get still. The Chaos Knight box also sold out quickly, but the rest are still live and kicking if you want to jump into one of the factions, though I may steer you away from the Blood Angels box, it simply looks kinda sad. If you missed our review of the new battleforces, you can find them here.

Innes Wilson (white shirt) and Jack Murphy (USA shirt). Credit: Rob "TheChirurgeon" Jones.

Player Focus: Innes Wilson 

The current #1 player in the ITC/WGR, Innes is on a dominant streak this year, also holding the #1 rank in Stat Check's Elo scoring. He's currently the odds-on favorite coming into this year's World Championships and looking to break out this year and take home gold after failing to make it out of the group stage in 2025. Innes is an incredibly talented player who's won a number of majors and teams events this year and the current captain of Team Scotland. While often known for playing Space Marines or Genestealer Cults, he's known as one of the best faction hoppers in the game and has recently been tearing it up with Death Guard - he can perform well with pretty much any faction in the game. Innes is also a writer for Tabletop Battles, so look up some of his Warhound-exclusive articles here or the Stat Check podcast if you want to hear from him more directly.

Innes is on a dominant streak this year; currently holding both number one ELO and ITC, he is the favorite coming into WCW. Winning a number of majors and teams events, Innes is an incredibly talented player who is known as one of the best faction hoppers in the game. While often known for his Space Marines, Innes can perform well with pretty much any faction in the game and tell you why you were playing the faction wrong. Innes is also one of our writers here at Tabletop Battles so take a look at some of his Warhound-exclusive articles or the Stat Check podcast if you want to hear from him directly.

Alongside our coverage of the whats-what of 40k each week, Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson joins us to provide some quick updates on the movers and shakers in the competitive scene of some of the other games we cover here at Tabletop Battles!

Tomb Kings and Blood Bowl Goblins Up for Preview

Big news for scary skeletons and silly little guys, as this week’s pre-order preview on Warhammer Community shows that we can expect new Old World Tomb Kings and Blood Bowl Goblins very soon.

The Tomb King release makes available separately most of the items that were released alongside the recent Tomb Kings reinforcements box, including resculpts of a wide array of the Skeleton models that makes up the bulk of the Tomb Kings line infantry and cavalry options. Alongside this wave of releases comes a new Arcane Journal, The Doom of Lord Carrard, which adds new options for both Bretonnians and Tomb Kings, as well as a new Army box for Tomb Kings featuring a new Skeleton sculpts and an all new Royal Herald sculpt, both mounted and on foot.

Meanwhile, in a very different part of the world-that-was, the Night Goblins are bouncing onto the Blood Bowl pitch with their new team, the Eight Peaks Loonatics. Consisting of Night Goblins, Squigs, and even several Night Goblins riding Squigs, the Loonatics lean on bending the rules and wacky play to bounce around the other team to victory. Alongside the new team and their accessories, Games Workshop is also releasing two new Star Players, the hulking Troll with a mind for ball Ripper Bogrot and the craziest, dizziest Night Goblin player of them all, Fungus the Loon.

All of these items will go on pre-order this Saturday, with a full release on December 5th.

The US Drives the Weekend’s Biggest AoS Events

We had not one, but two large Age of Sigmar GTs over the weekend, one singles and one teams, both of them coming to you hot from the North American region.

For singles, the Oklahoma Open (OKO) was easily the largest singles event of the entire weekend, drawing 76 players over five rounds. The final results is another win for the elves of the Mortal Realms, but this time with way less trees like we saw with last weekend’s results and this time with way more murder. While there were two undefeated players at this event, Wyatt Moran’s Daughters of Khaine took 1st place from battle points, with Moran leaning on Morathi, a big block of Blood Sisters and a big block of Witch Aelves to get work done. The other undefeated was Justin Foster on Khazalite Holds, bringing in the newest faction with a bang by bringing in a tough brick of Gholems supported by a wide range of goodstuff and even Gotrek for some Fyreslayers flair.

Meanwhile, the Old Town Throwdown was a 100 player teams event over the weekend held in California. After the dust settled, out of 20 teams represented only 1 team emerged undefeated, TSD Horde Sucks, Alliance FTW. While their taste in Horde versus Alliance is objectively wrong, their team composition wasn’t at all, featuring Flesh Eater Courts, Stormcast, Idoneth Deepkin, Soulblight, and Maggotkin. Congratulations to the TSD team for the win, as well as to Wyatt and Justin for their undefeated performances at OKO!

Poland Celebrates Da Red Gobbo with a Kill Team Teams GT

The folks over in the Polish Kill Team Metagame broke what was a quiet few weeks for Kill Team while we wait for new Approved Ops with one of the largest teams events we’ve seen for Kill Team in a while, Da Red Gobbo Tournament - Drużynowe Mistrzostwa Polski. This event had 72 players all divided up into 3 man teams, who played over 6 rounds for the top spot. Competition at the event was fierce, with no team ending a true undefeated record. The 1st place team did get pretty close though, with Lubikon I taking the top spot with a 5-0-1 record. The team composition featured Canoptek, Raveners, and Spectre Squad, which gives Lubikon a healthy variety of maps and teams that they can play into well no matter the matchup. Canoptek are generally good no matter the map or matchup, while Raveners remain a terror on Tomb World even after the nerfs and Spectre Squad when played well are extremely hard to pin down on Volkus. Congratulations to the Lubikon I crew for the big win for Da Red Gobbo!

Protoss Starter by Blake Law

StarCraft Breaks Into GT World with Huge Polish Event

We’re right back to Poland with our next event to look at, this time leaving the world of Warhammer 40,000 and into the world of StarCraft.

Likely ranking as the largest starCraft Miniatures Game event to date with 93 players, the Oficjalne Mistrzostwa Polski StarCraft Tabletop Miniatures Game took place over five rounds and saw players bring two 2k point lists from the same faction, one of the two lists to be selected each match up. Despite a slow start out of the gate, the recent buffs to Zerg were enough to push them into a competitive spot with Klusek piloting them to the top spot and an undefeated record. While Klusek changed around his upgrades used in each list, his main army core remained the same between both, leaning on plenty of vilelings, a bile launcher and hydralisks for ranged support, and the two hero dream team of both Kerrigan and Zagara for plenty of mayhem. Congratulations to Klusek on the win!

Rebel Forces Take Star Wars Legion Gold at OKO

We’re ending the same place we started today over in Oklahoma for the Oklahoma Open Legion GT, one of the largest events for the recently revitalized Star Wars Legion from Atomic Mass Games (AMG).

The event, which is a part of the official tournament circuit for AMG, took place over six rounds, with players bringing 1000 point army lists to the competition for first prize. While there was representation from all of the games factions, the Rebels in particular did extremely well at OKO alongside the Mandalorians, with both factions each taking 3 of the top 8 spots. The Rebels edged out the Mandalorians in the end though, with Colton Evans winning first place as the sole undefeated of the event. His list leaned heavily on some of the most iconic heroes of Star Wars, like Luke Skywalker, Han Solo, and Lando Carlrissian, with some specialist infantry and an AT-RT to support, which was enough to beat out Aidan Cone’s Republic forces in game six to take home the gold. Congratulations to Colton for taking home the top spot!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don’t forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website and more.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Huron's Marauders (Updated November 16, 2026)
content:
In this series of articles we take a deep dive into a specific Detachment for a faction, covering the faction’s rules and upgrades and talking about how to build around that faction for competitive play. In this article, we’re covering the Huron’s Marauders Detachment for Chaos Space Marines.

The Maelstrom campaign supplement gave Chaos Space Marines two new Detachments to work with, both modeled after the renegade marines who fled to the Maelstrom. Huron’s Marauders is the more Huron-focused of the two Detachments, pushing players to build around Huron but adding plenty of value and versatility without requiring you to give up Dark Pacts. If you want to play renegades but don’t want to give up Dark Pacts, this may be the Detachment for you.

Changelog

  • 11-16-2026 (Current): Updated for 11th edition
  • 02-11-2026: Initial Publication

Detachment Cost: 3 DP

Dispositions: Disruption, Purge the Foe

The Huron’s Marauders Detachment is designed to model the jaded raiding forces of Huron Blackheart; it’s an infantry-focused Detachment which improves your Infantry damage output with +1 to hit or the ability to fall back and shoot or charge (or both if Huron can see them), and has some solid ways to buff damage on both charging units and Damned units. The real value here however is movement tricks: This Detachment has a ton of different ways to move and position against an opponent, from an Enhancement that gives you Infiltrators to Stratagems that let you auto-advance 6”, make a surge move, or go back into reserves. There’s a ton of value here for veteran players who know how to use movement to their advantage.

As a 3 DP Detachment, you give up a lot of added value to take this Detachment, and you're banking big on the value of those Detachment rules. Which, to be fair - are pretty good. The other upside here is that you get access to the Purge the Foe Disposition, which is something Chaos Space Marines generally struggle to access - the only other place you can get it is in the 3 DP Creations of Bile Detachment. CSM tend to be a glass cannon army, so it's not a bad Detachment for them to sport.

Detachment Rule: Tyrannical Motivation

In your Command phase, you pick one of two abilities. Until the start of your next Command phase, all HERETIC ASTARTES INFANTRY units in your army gain the selected ability. At the start of each phase, if one of those units is visible to your Huron Blackheart model, they have both abilities.

The two abilities are:

  • +1 to Hit
  • Fall back and shoot/charge

This is pretty powerful. Getting +1 to hit is just generically good across the board, especially on units like Terminators, Mutilators, Obliterators, Legionaries, and Red Corsairs Raiders, while cult units like Plague Marines and Noise Marines also really like that bonus. Being able to fall back and shoot/charge is also great and being able to switch to it in key situations but keeping +1 to hit active for your army on most rounds gives you just enough flexibility. When you combine it with [SUSTAINED HITS 1], which is mathematically identical to +1 to hit, you can get some solid conversion rates for your firepower, which is even more valuable in a post-S5 AP-1 bolters world.

Because this just hits your Infantry, it also acts as a solid buff on your DAMNED units, and so this is another Detachment where Accursed Cultists, Traitor Guardsmen, and Beastmen can really shine. Accursed Cultists really benefit from getting +1 to hit in melee on the turns when they aren't using your Cult Demagogue's Dark Ritual ability and being able to go to +2 to get around -1 to hit is also pretty great.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Enhancements

There are two real options here: Raid Leader and Eager for Bloodshed, which let you set up some very nasty strategies. Raid Leader is the more notable of the two, and the one to build around. The big challenge you're going to have is going to be taking non-named characters to throw these on.

  • Voice of the Tyrant (25 points) – Non-DAMNED model only. The bearer’s unit gets both abilities from the Tyrannical Motivation Detachment rule. This is pretty great, as it means your bearer’s unit always gets +1 to hit and the ability to fall back and charge. This can let you skirt some of the restrictions on the Detachment rule - if you give a Lord Discordant or Daemon Prince this Enhancement, they’ll be able to benefit from the effects when they normally wouldn’t. That said, they won’t do much for you with this upgrade, so it’s best on something attached to a unit like Terminators.
  • Raid Leader (20 points) – Goes on a non-DAMNED model. Each time the bearer’s unit is set up after disembarking from a TRANSPORT that made a normal move this turn, they’re still eligible to declare a charge. This is very good, giving you the ability to move up with a Rhino, then pop out and charge. Huge on a unit of Raiders, who otherwise lack the sweet Advance and Charge chosen get, and plenty good on Chosen as well. Being able to go 15” before you charge gives you a huge threat range to work with.
  • Dread Reputation (25 points) – Goes on a non-DAMNED model. Each time the bearer’s unit is set up on the table, each enemy unit within 6” of the bearer’s unit - or 12” if you set up with DEEP STRIKE - has to take a Battle-shock test. This is cute, and can hit a lot of units, but isn’t super-reliable and is only like to be used once per game unless you combine it with the ability to go back into reserves.
  • Eager for Bloodshed (30 points) – The bearer has the INFILTRATORS ability. This is very good. There are the standard, boring uses - putting a regular Chaos Lord or Master of Executions with a unit of Raiders, for example - but the real fun is on large solo characters. Think Lord Discordant and Daemon Prince, two big units that would love some easier turn 1 charges. The Daemon Prince in particular can infiltrate and stay close to Raiders to maintain Lone Operative until it’s time to cause problems. You can do a lot with this enhancement, though you're going to be limited by the terrain layouts - Infiltrating in 11th Edition can get you killed pretty easily if you aren't careful.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Stratagems

The Stratagems here are very solid. There’s a lot of good utility in these and more than half of them are movement tricks.

  • Hardened Killers (Battle Tactic, 1 CP) – Used in your Command phase on a DAMNED unit in your army. Pick one effect from : +1 BS, +1 attack on rapid fire weapons, or +1 to saves. This is a clear nod to the orders that Astra Militarum get, giving the analogous options to Take Aim!, First Rank, Fire! Second Rank, Fire!, and Take Cover!, and these are all really good, especially on units with t-shirts and BS4+. Traitor Guard are the obvious pick for this (and +1 shot will usually be better than +1 to hit), but it’s not bad in a pinch on something like Accursed Cultists if you’re going up against AP0 guns in cover and you can suddenly turn that into a 4+ save. But that’s also a great benefit for Traitor Guardsmen as well, who get cover while they’re within range of an objective and would love to be working with an effective 3+ save. Note that, unlike orders, you can use this, then become Battle-shocked and you won’t lose the effect.
  • At the Tyrant’s Command (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in your Movement phase on a non-MONSTER, non-VEHICLE unit. That unit can shoot and charge this turn even after it Advanced. This is not the ideal timing for the Stratagem - you cant' double up on this and Seize the Prize - but it’s still insanely strong, even if locked to Infantry. It’s amazing on Raiders, Mutiliators, Terminators, Raptors, Warp Talons, and Possessed, all of whom really like the extra speed. It’s also pretty great on Obliterators, who can really use a bit of extra movement before shooting.
  • Seize the Prize (Battle Tactic, 1 CP) – Used in your Movement phase on a non-MONSTER, non-VEHICLE unit that has been picked to Advance. It can automatically advance 6” instead of rolling. Unfortunately, this is a Movement phase Stratagem so you can't combine it with At the Tyrant's Command but it's perfect for a unit of Chosen, who already have that built-in ability to advance and charge. 6" of auto movement is a huge boost, and knowing you can reliably press forward can be great for flipping objectives late in the game.
  • Reavers’ Flurry (Battle Tactic, 1 CP) – Used in your Fight phase on a unit that charged this turn. That unit gets +1 Attacks with its melee weapons. This is really, really good. It flat out improves your output on most models by 25% to 33% and gets better the more models you have in the unit. It’s particularly amazing on Chosen and Mutilators and not too shabby on Terminators, Raiders, Possessed, and Raptors. 
  • To the Favoured the Spoils (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in your opponent’s Shooting phase after one of their units shoots. Pick one of your units that lost a wound from that unit’s attacks and they can make a Surge move, going up to D6”. They have to move as close as possible to the closest enemy unit, and can end up within Engagement Range of that unit. This is another really great tool, and great for threatening opponents with - you’d be surprised how often people will choose not to shoot you at all if it means getting hit off-turn and it forces them to carefully consider their shooting sequencing. This one isn't restricted to vehicles, and that means you can use it to properly punish opponents who want to take pot shots at a transport, moving to block them or even engage them and preventing them from charging a key unit.
  • Encircling Surge (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used at the end of your opponent’s Fight phase. One of your non-MONSTER, non-VEHICLE units within 6” of the battlefield and outside Engagement range of an enemy unit can go back into Reserves. This is more restrictive than some uppy-downy effects but still incredibly good. Note that you don’t have to be “wholly within,” only within, so a single model just needs to be toeing that line to get your unit back up into orbit. This can be a good way to get insurance with a unit of Warp Talons or make the most out of bikes or Raptors. Also can combine with Dread Reputation if you’re a sicko trying to force multiple tests per game.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

This Detachment feels like a variation on the themes of Renegade Raiders, pushing you toward Infantry and transports with lots of Movement tools to help you get around the table and an always-on buff to your offensive output. The Detachment rule only having an effect on INFANTRY means you’ll be pushed to using those units, but the good news is that those tend to be some of the faction’s best non-Defiler units anyways. The changes to CSM datasheets in 11th edition have made Terminators some of the army's best units, and they're very good in this Detachment, enjoying +1 to hit and the ability to advance and charge. You may not be able to get the S6 bolter shots out of them you enjoy with Cabal of Chaos, but massed S5 AP-1 fire - boosted to AP-2 with Death Hex - is still pretty good on its own.

You can also get a lot of power out of Chosen and Mutilators here, especially when you combine +1 to hit with SUSTAINED HITS 1 from Dark Pacts. Huron's very good here, but you don't necessarily need him - getting both abilities while you can see him is great but if all you did was take the +1 to hit every turn you'd be fine. Huron's kind of a 50/50 character prospect compared to other options for both Terminators (Kravek Morne, Terminator Sorcerer), and Chosen (Fabius Bile).

This is one of the few Detachments which boosts DAMNED units and Traitor Guardsmen in particular get a ton of value here - they can suddenly become pretty nasty when they hit on 3+ with extra Rapid Fire shots and having OC 2 makes them annoyingly good at stealing objectives, especially when you remember that they can auto-advance 6” with Seize the Prize. Having improved DAMNED units gives this army the powerful ability to throw out and trade cheap chaff units - something Chaos Space Marine armies can often struggle with outside of Chaos Cult lists.  Accursed Cultists are also great here, as they can stay accurate on other turns instead of relying too heavily on a single turn of Demagogue buffs to actually score damage.

With an infantry focus, one of your big challenges here is going to be how you handle armor and harder saves - CSM struggle to get better than AP-2 with their melee output and don’t have much damage 3, either. You can cover some of these gaps with Obliterators and Havocs, both of which benefit from the +1 to hit in the Detachment rule and can make good use of At the Tyrant’s Command Stratagem to advance and shoot. Havcos' ability to ignore cover helps a ton here, as it means they're just hitting their targets on a 2+ all the time. This makes Lascannon Havocs actually viable, able to stay hidden until they need to light a vehicle up.

I really like Obliterators in this Detachment, where the ability to go back into reserves with Encircling Surge means they can drop in near a table edge, shoot something, then pull back up at the end of your opponent's turn, making them ready to drop in again and light up another target. The +1 to hit also helps them maximize their damage output and avoid the challenges of 11th edition cover while the ability to fall back and shoot in a pinch stops them from getting into too much trouble.

Strengths

  • Movement. You have a ton of movement tricks here, from built-in fall back and shoot/charge to Advance and Charge, uppy downy, and auto advance 6”, plus if you’re taking Huron he comes with his own built-in reactive move. You have a ton of ways to get around the table and move out of phase.
  • Offensive output. A flat +1 to hit across your army is really good. It’s like having Sustained Hits 1 on all the time for your units that hit on 3+ and will frustrate armies relying on -1 to be hit. Reavers’ Flurry further boosts this.
  • Damned units. It’s not often you see a Detachment which can help out Damned units and Traitor Guardsmen in particular are great in this Detachment, getting both passive buffs and a Stratagem tailored to evoke the powerful Orders rules for Astra Militarum.

Weaknesses

  • Vehicles. There’s almost nothing here to help Vehicles, and you’ll still likely want one or two of those to handle bigger threats.
  • Anti-Armor Output. On a similar note, your ability to take out heavier threats is going to be a bit limited - most of your melee infantry have AP-2 attacks and no way to improve that in this Detachment, which can make taking down bigger threats an issue. 
  • Infantry-focused. There are some good buffs here for infantry - but the game is pretty lethal right now for armies of 2W and even 3W infantry, and the same lists that are tooled to kill Victrix are going to do just fine into Possessed, Chosen, and Raiders.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

A Sample List

We haven't seen a ton of success for Huron's Marauders lists in 11th edition, in part because CSM lists tend to focus on Cabal of Chaos right now. However, these lists are solid in teams events, where they can be very capable options for your Purge the Foe Disposition. This list comes from Euan Bedford-Cooper, who took it to the Autumn International Team Tournament in November and finished 5-0, with a 12-8 win over Vik Vijay's Adepta Sororitas (Disruption) in round 5.

title: Narrative Forge: Five Leagues from the Mortal Realms - Part 1
content:
Our “Narrative Forge” hobby articles exist to encourage stretching yourself out in the hobby - and that includes trying new games and rules. But those can be quite a commitment... unless you use what you already have! Today, Hydriatus takes a look at using Five Leagues From The Borderlands forge a narrative for your Age of Sigmar collection! This first part covers the character creation and setting setup for a campaign. 

Released in 2022, the 3rd edition of Five Leagues From The Borderlands offers a comprehensive set of solo rules to play out the adventures of a warband in a frontier setting. Designed for model agnostic play on a 2'x2' or 3'x3' board, it offers an RPG-lite experience with a procedurally generated campaign world.

Perfect for our purposes - forging a narrative to go with an Age of Sigmar army!

Five Leagues From The Borderlands Rulebook. (Credit - Modiphius)

I've recently been working on a Slaves to Darkness force, using a mix of Age of Sigmar, Old World, and third party miniatures to fit my theme of a Darkoath Tribe hailing from the frozen plains of Bjarl in the Realm of Ghur - whose story we will flesh out with the help of a solo Five Leagues From The Borderlands campaign!

What We Need

To begin, we'll need:

  • The Five Leagues From The Borderlands rulebook.
  • Enough miniatures to represent your warband and some foes. Any two-player starter set will furnish you with enough, or the equivalent of a Warcry box for your warband and a  Spearhead for your foes.
  • A board and scenery - while officially the game is designed for 2'x2' or 3'x3', it works just as well on a Spearhead board! You will need way more scenery than a Spearhead set comes with though.

The Rules

Playing the game itself is simple - characters roll for initiative at the start of a round, with the result and their Agility determining their order of activation alongside the enemies. Models first move and then either perform a combat action or a non-combat action (like running or casting magic). After every model has activated, there is a tracking phase during which morale checks are carried out and reinforcements appear.

Combat involves rolling a D6, adding the model's Combat Skill, and meeting/beating a target number. If successful, you then roll another D6 and compare it to the target's armor - if you match the number, the target is stunned. If you beat the number, you roll another D6 and compare that to the target's Toughness - if you beat it, they are removed from play. If you meet the number or roll under, they are wounded and stunned, and on a natural 1 they are just stunned.

(Stunned figures have penalties in melee, making it easier to wound and slay them with a follow up. If a wounded model would become wounded again, they are removed from play.)

Magic is handled differently - you roll 2D6 plus the model's Casting Skill, and try to meet or beat the target number associated with the spell you want to cast. This works the same as background skills, which you can make during the campaign phase to try to obtain resources or information or otherwise progress your adventure.

The Characters

In Five Leagues From The Borderlands, you create a skirmish warband who wander around a region dealing with random encounters (tabletop battles).

Your warband consists of 6 characters, represented by suitable miniatures - 4 heroes and 2 followers. Each character has a stat line consisting of Agility, Speed, Combat Skill, Toughness, and Casting Ability (if they are the Mystic archetype). They also have a number of skills based on their origin and background, which you can roll against to help with preparing for a battle or recovering after one.

Origins and backgrounds also grant various stat increases, special abilities, equipment, or skills. Wealth and equipment is generated individually for each character, but can be pooled and reallocated.

Once the 4 heroes are generated, you pick one to be your Avatar, which grants it more Will and Luck, as well as some randomly generated backstory. This is, for all intents and purposes, your warband leader.

As Five Leagues is based on low-fantasy, fairly small encounters, it makes sense to build your warband out of a single unit option. As I was building up my army for games of Spearhead at first, I chose to base my warband on my eventual unit of Darkoath Savagers. As the basic Savagers miniatures did not match the winter theme I was going for, I turned to mostly using Old World Chaos Marauders as a basis, with some Darkoath models from Warhammer Underworlds mixed in to represent the models supposed to be on different sized bases within the unit. And because I wanted a clear leader, I chose to add my Darkoath Warqueen as well - because I think the model looks cool and makes a nice focal point for a warband.

Vizhna and her companions embark upon the Path to Glory! (Credit - Hydriatus)

Character Creation

With my miniatures chosen, it was time to figure out how to represent them within the game itself.

Vizhna, the Inheritor

First of all, the leader, the Warqueen Vhizna - who I named after a quick glance at a Darkoath name generator I found online! A quick glance at the available character creation options helped me figure out how best to represent her on the table - a Human Zealot.

In Five Leagues, Humans get a bonus to Speech tests, and are the only origin capable of attaining more than one point of Will - an in-game resource that can be spent during battles for various one-off bonuses and effects. Perfect to represent a "main character". Meanwhile, the Zealot background (only available to Humans) makes it likely for a character to start with extra Luck, as if they are favored by some Dark Power...

Each background has a series of D20 tables you can roll on to to determine the character's Capabilities, Mentality, Possessions, and Training. I took my D20, made some rolls, and got the following results:

  • Agility Increase
  • +1XP
  • Basic Weapon
  • 1 Skill (Leadership)

From these results, we can see Vizhna is more focused on dexterity and mobility than raw power. She also has some experience, implying she has been prepared for this adventure - trained by a parent, an elder of the tribe or current leader perhaps? She brings a fairly basic weapon with her to add to the stash, but clearly knows how to command warriors and convince them to join her cause - maybe she was a unit leader during previous raids, and now undertakes a quest to prove herself to the tribe that she can command a raid herself?

Vizhna. (Credit - Hydriatus)

As she is my "main character", she is designated the Avatar and gains a free point of Luck and Will, before rolling on the Avatar History table and getting the "Old Map" result. This adds a Hidden Delve (dungeon) to our eventual region map - and just like that, we have a storyline and campaign goal! Our hero will have to decipher the old map, locate the dungeon, and plunder it for whatever treasures lie within!

Vizhna is a warrior of the Blood Claw tribe, who has been on her share of raids. Now however, the time has come for her to take her first steps on the Path to Glory. During her last raid, she uncovered a curious map written in a foreign scrawl. Swearing an Oath to discover the map's secrets, she sets out with a small group of companions to earn the attention of the Gods... 

Taulveg, the Smith

Next, my proxy Darkoath Savager Slaughterborn, Dendrel from Brand's Oathbound. Essentially a unit champion for the Savagers, I chose to make my Slaughterborn a smith instead, responsible for issuing out the finest weapons to proven warriors, and the unit being his bodyguards. As this campaign is a prequel of sorts to my army's lore, he would be accompanying Vizhma to collect equipment for the tribe, and maybe even find a worthy relic or two to inspire his own work.

Wanting some variety, I looked at my character creation options and found the Preen - foul-tempered avians with a bonus to Crafting tests. They also are forced to take the Townsfolk background, which is focused around wealth. Perfect for my purposes.

I rolled on the relevant tables, and ended up with the following:

  • Speed Increase
  • +1 XP
  • 3 Gold marks
  • 1 Skill (Battlewise)
Taulveg. (Credit - Hydriatus)

That struck me as a someone probably falling under the influence of Slaanesh, swift to get to grips with the foe (although Khorne would also work in terms of narrative)! Taulveg clearly has spent time in battle before, and maybe was part of Vizhna's unit before she took her Oath and embarked on this quest. He was must also have been a successful raider, amassing a small personal fortune, and knew how to read the tide of battle.

(Although with such a speed, I probably could have substituted a mounted model instead and themed it as a fellrider!)

Taulveg is one of the few smiths in the Blood Claws. While most of the tribe's equipment come from raids, they still require craftsmen to maintain and repair it equipment - and Taulveg has an eye for the material that makes him perfectly suited for such a role. Having served under Vizhna's command in past raids, he has come along on the adventure out of loyalty, and a chance to claim a share of the spoils the mysterious map is bound to lead Vizhna to...

Ikherd, the God-Speaker

The Mortal Realms are a very magical setting, so it seemed obvious to include some kind of spellcasting character - and a Savager unit does come with a God-speaker! Besides, a potential Warqueen on a quest is bound to draw the Gods' attention, so it simply made sense to have her accompanied by someone who could interpret signs from the Four.

This particular model is from the Warhammer: Underworlds Gnarlspirit Pack, a collection of very nice Ghur-themed Darkoath who only need a little conversion work to make suitable for the winter climes my army was themed around!

In the interest of exploring all the options available, I chose a Fey-Blood origin for the mystic, as it comes with a Foresight ability and an aura preventing opponents from gaining bonuses against the character. Ideal to represent the foreboding aura of someone who dabbles in Chaos magic!

Ikherd. (Credit- Hydriatus)

My rolls on the Mystic tables gave me the following:

  • Casting Increase
  • +1 XP
  • Mystic Item (2 Congealed Strands)
  • Alchemy Skill

Clearly, this is someone who hasn't been on as many raids as the others, but rather stayed back in the village making poultices and salves. However, clearly they are favored by Tzeentch if they find casting spells easier than others.

Speaking of spells, I rolled for the 3 starting spells and got:

  • Distract
  • Premonition
  • Forsee

Then for my 2 choices, I selected

  • Heal
  • Guidance

Ikherd clearly is a seer of some kind!

Part of the coterie that attends the tribe's shaman, Ikherd was a lowly assistant entrusted with the medical care of the wounded after each raid. After he proved capable of pre-empting shortages in supplies, the tribe's shaman recognized the man's aptitude for magic and taught him how to commune with spirits. His insight and foretelling has become quite respected within the Blood Claws, so none challenged or questioned him when he declared his intent to accompany Vizhna to see her Oath carried out. 

Drifa, the Unbound

For my final character, I chose to make another melee-focused one as the Savager unit had one more non-basic model - the Wrathtouched. I used another proxy from the  Gnarlspirit Pack. It made a nice looking veteran monster hunter, fitting the aesthetic of my totally-not-Norscans.

Drifa. (Credit - Hydriatus)

This time, I chose a Duskling origin, which grants the Counter Attack ability against undead, a reroll to their attack on the charge, and a distrust of magic - so someone definitively choosing Khorne as their patron. Maybe a survivor of the Necroquake, or a veteran of battles against the Ossiarch Bonereapers who have been settling the continent of Bjarl.

The only background available to Dusklings is outsider, which focuses on self-sufficient survival. My rolls on the subtables this time gave me the following:

  • Toughness Increase
  • +1 XP
  • Fine Basic Weapon
  • 2 skills - Speech, Expertise

So a real veteran compared to everyone else in the warband, harder to wound, bearing a finely honed axe, and recognized for her skills at carousing and avoiding natural hazards.

Hailing from a tribe that was wiped out by the undead, Drifa bears an ever-burning hatred of those who serve Nagash. Though she survived the attack that saw her tribe annihilated and made her way west, upon reaching the territory of the Blood Claws she was treated as an outsider. Denied an opportunity to raid, she has joined Vizhna on her journey in exchange for a promise to be taken along on future raids should the Oath-quest be successful. 

Followers

In addition to the 4 heroes, a warband has 2 followers - minor supporting characters who may through their deeds one day become heroes of note themselves. These have a basic statline, and count as having the human origin, but receive no stat improvements. Rolling on the Follower table grants me the following personalities:

  • Studious Apprentice
  • Brave Villager

These made me think of two tribe members, probably unblooded who haven't even been on their first raid yet.

Finally, we have the warband's stash - their equipment and collected treasure.

  • 6 Gold (can be spent in settlements on equipment or further followers)
  • 2 Silvertree Leaf (used to speed-up post-battle healing)

The World

With our warband done, it was time to generate the world - or at least the setting of our narrative campaign.As I mentioned earlier, my Age of Sigmar Slaves to Darkness army is based on the continent of Bjarl, in the realm of Ghur - and I am using primarily the Old World Chaos Marauders as my models due to preferring their sculpts over the Darkoath for my rank-and-file winter warrior aesthetic.

A quick check on Lexicanum gave me a map of Bjarl to use as a basis - but as Bjarl is a whole continent, I was somewhat spoilt for choice! I decided to come back to this stage after I had more an idea of what would be required on the map itself, and proceeded through the next steps of setting up a campaign for Five Leagues.

Ghurish Heartlands. (Credit - Games Workshop)

While any options can be chosen to make the kind of campaign you want to play, I chose to randomly generate all my options and see what I could make out of them. The first roll I made was to determine who settled the region I would be exploring was - and rolled low, so there would be only two settlements, a Village (with a market town specialization) and a town (with the Manor specialization).

Well, the number is fitting considering Bjarl is often described as a brutal place, mostly inhabited by nomadic Chaos and Ogor tribes. Still, a village established enough to be recognized a fledgling trade hub in Ghur... well, to me, that seemed to indicate a port town, somewhere the nomads could gather and trade every couple of seasons - a place where harvested beast parts would be exchanged for rare worked metal tools and weapons.

As for a community gathered around the manor of a local noble, which has the mechanical effect of allowing you to repair 2 items rather than one per visit... well, that sounded like a place of exiles, gathered around a disgraced noble who was forced south. Probably the ruler of the small port village as well!

Next, I determined the threats facing the region. Again, I chose to randomly determine these rather than choose. My results were:

  • The Whispers from Beyond (undead and cultists)
  • The Ice-heart Court (tree-folk and fey)
  • The Faceless Kingdom (disciplined military forces)

...I don't know about you, but to me that sounds like:

  • Anything from Grand Alliance: Death
  • Sylvaneth
  • Cities of Sigmar / Stormcast Eternals
A soldier from Coldfort pays their respects to a fallen comrade. (Credit - Hydriatus)

From there, I quickly browsed through Lexicanum again and found the two Bonereaper settlements in eastern Bjarl, and a Sigmarite stronghold in the north-west Bjarl known as Coldfort. And I had already generated an entire town of people gathered around the leadership of an exiled noble, it made sense to be closer to Coldfort. That meant the north-west of Bjarl. Glancing at a map of the Ghurish Heartlands, I found the place for my campaign - the Bloodwhiten Fjords...

...and that's all we have space for in this article! Join me next time, when the Campaign gets going and I provide some examples of play!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? title: MTG card size and dimensions explained
content:
Ever wondered what the standard MTG card size is? It's not a question that plagues Magic: The Gathering fans often, but it can be very helpful to know in a few crucial situations. Whether you're a top-level player looking to swot up or simply a lover of Wizards of the Coast trivia, we can tell you all there is to know about MTG card dimensions below.

Before we answer those burning questions, though, here are a few other handy guides for the avid TCG fan. All the latest news can be found in the MTG release schedule, and we're constantly updating our guide to the MTG Arena codes.

But back to size - and why it matters.

How big is an MTG card?

According to the official Magic: The Gathering rules, a 'traditional' MTG card size is 2.5 inches (6.3cm) by 3.5 inches (8.8cm). Non-foil cards are roughly 0.012 inches (0.305mm) thick, and foil cards are fractionally thicker.

Printing errors aside, there are some exceptions. These come under the category of 'non-traditional cards' in the official Magic rules. One example includes cards from the 1997 Vanguard MTG set, which were three inches by five inches.

What does an MTG card weigh?

The standard Magic card weight is somewhere between 1.7 and 1.8 grams. There will of course be some variation (printing isn't perfect), but this is the rough ballpark any authentic MTG card will be in.

 

Why does MTG card size matter?

Competitive play

An MTG card's dimensions are particularly important for competitive players, as cards with a uniform size help to prevent cheating. According to tournament rules, any card that is markedly different from the others in an MTG deck is considered an illegal, marked card. And though it isn't one of the specific examples listed by Magic judges, card size differences could be considered a form of marking.

The best thing to do is to sleeve your cards. Any card could differ from standard sizing due to printing errors, so sleeves help keep everything uniform.

Spotting fakes

The most expensive MTG cards can be worth hundreds of thousands of dollars, so it helps to know what the real ones look like. Sizing is just one of many factors that might be considered when checking if a card is real or counterfeit.

Here the size of everything on the card counts. This doesn't just include the general dimensions - understanding the size and spacing of font, art, and borders can all help identify a legitimate card, too. One or two mistakes could be a misprint, but several may indicate something suspicious.

MTG playmat size

There's no official MTG playmat size according to the comprehensive Magic: The Gathering rules. However, if you're still curious, the average size is 24 inches by 14 inches (61.0 cm by 35.6 cm).

MTG deck size

An MTG deck size depends on which of the formats you're playing. Constructed formats like Standard and Modern require a minimum of 60 cards, but there's no maximum deck size. If you have a sideboard, this can include up to 15 cards.

In a limited format like an draft, the standard deck size is 40 cards at the minimum. Again, there's no maximum deck size. And this time, there's also no size restrictions for your sideboard.

MTG maximum hand size

The maximum hand size in a Magic: The Gathering game is usually seven cards. If you have more than seven cards in your hand during the cleanup step, you must discard down to seven. There are exceptions - certain cards can alter your hand size during play.

Need more of the nooks and crannies of MTG explained? You can ask as many questions as you like in our official Wargamer Discord. As long as they're about Magic, that is. We probably can't help you with that weird rash…

title: Trench Crusade's newest minis include Leper Pilgrims, Naval Raiders, and a crab with a hand grenade
content:
Trench Crusade has revealed two new plastic model kits that expand on the killer miniatures that came in the Carcass Front box set - crazed Leper Pilgrims of the Procession of the Sacred Affliction, and the depraved Heretic Raiders who make up the mainstay of the elite Heretic Naval Raiders force. The new kits provide additional basic infantry for both warbands, and most excitingly come with a plethora of additional weapons and equipment - including a crab with a grenade.

Both sets are multipart plastic kits that build five models, and are available to pre-order for $39.99 / £29.99 on the Trench Crusade webstore. According to the store description, "shipping of pre-orders will begin mid December, with stores receiving their stock shortly after", and will ship "from hubs in the EU, the UK and the USA". Orders might arrive in time for Christmas, though there's a risk they'll be blitzed by the seasonal rush on the postal service.

When I built the previous round of Naval Raiders and Sacred Affliction kits for my Carcass Front review, I found that the quality of engineering was on par with Games Workshop's models. That's just as well, because $8 per human-sized mini is a very Games Workshop sort of price.

1/4

These kits do seem to be very, very good for kitbashing - the shop listings on the Trench Crusade webstore list a lot of cool weapon options and oddball equipment. To pick out a few bits and pieces on the Leper Pilgrims, my eyes are drawn to the banner, a crucifix with the remains of an Ecclesiastical Prisoner nailed to it, and a fantastic new Punt Gun that allows you to give the warband's oversized blunderbuss to a pilgrim with the Zealot Strength upgrade, instead of to the Castigator.

The loot is particularly rich for the well-armed and elite Heretic Raiders. Their haul includes three SMGs and a machine gun to absolutely blanket your opponent in bullets, a musical instrument to make your troops practically incapable of failing a Dash test, and the ultimate in fashion - a cape with an entire shark on top. And of course there's the crab with a potato-masher hand grenade in one claw. Inspired.

There have been 3D printable expansions for both warbands already including Leper Knights, the tentacular Leviathal Chorus, and an upgrade set to make a Sacred Affliction variant of the Shrine Anchorite. Both warbands are still waiting on a few key releases: the mine-chucking Sea Hag, additional elite Anointed, and luckless Wretched for the Raiders; and the superhuman Communicant, additional Stygmatic Nuns, and (equally luckless) Ecclesiastic prisoners for the Sacred Affliction.

Wargamer's editor Mollie spent a lot of time talking to the team at Factory Fortress Inc about Trench Crusade during this year's Essen Spiel. I wrote up her interview with Chief Operating Officer Jamie Sutcliffe to learn how well the team is keeping up with unexpected demand. At the time he promised monthly releases (with a break for Christmas) - it seems that the studio is on track so far.

If you've got a Trench Crusade Warband, why not share your pics in the Wargamer Discord community?

title: Hobby Build Academy: Holiday Gift Advice
content:
With less than two weeks till Black Friday and the crush of holiday shopping begins in earnest, your Hobby Build Academy faculty have been talking about how to prepare for holiday gifting, but not in the sense of where to buy or find deals, but more how to help guide those who aren't hobby familiar to getting gifts at both a good cost and for what you actually need; sometimes, getting the right gift from someone can have almost as many hardships as getting the right gift FOR another person. This can be especially true if you're dealing with extended family or friends who aren't that into what you do for a hobby, and while we'll be talking about Gunpla, LEGO and other model kits today, this advice can probably serve just about anyone who gets asked "what would you like for the holidays"?

Marcy: So, you and I are pretty good gift givers, I think; you certainly always manage to surprise people and put a lot of thought into things, and I've always felt like it takes some skill to be a considerate gifter.

Elly: I mean, the idea is that you're giving people something they want, but also something that says "hey, I thought about you", so... it goes to reason that you should probably be putting some decent thought into the things you buy?

Marcy: Right. Well, you've met my family, and I've met yours, so...

Elly: ...Yeah. Let's just leave it at "Not everyone is good at gifts."

Marcy: I also think that sometimes people can easily overlook that when people are not in a community or hobby space of some sort, relying on other people to find gifts for your special interest places a lot of labor on that person to produce something they may not have any idea about, let alone access to, and that taking some time to consider their feelings can be the difference between a thoughtful gift and something that was a last minute hail mary.

Elly: Yeahhhhhh. Relying on Amazon to just solve all of your problems is not the way to go,  but sometimes when people really don't know what else to do and it says the item will arrive tomorrow, it can be an easy go tfo. So, we figured we'd try to make it easier by coming up with some tips for people to think about regarding hobby stuff before people start doing their shopping; a lot of people do almost all of it right at the start of the season, so this is probably right on time!

Make a List

Okay, so the first tip is pretty obvious: make a list for people to work off of. Make the list in order of priority and then be sure to give it to people in a method that actually works for them; if they don't shop on Amazon, don't hand them an Amazon wishlist. If they don't know what a "Google Drive" is, don't send them a Sheets file with your color coded wishlist. Figure out what works best for the people you are giving it to, and organize it based off of what you want, but also how they'll best understand it.

Marcy: My mother would almost always only look at the top five items on a wishlist, no matter how many notes or otherwise I added to it; she just went for whatever she saw first and then clicked down the line before calling it a day.

Elly: Mine barely even looked at lists except to look at the price!

Marcy: And, well, we aren't doing family therapy this week but I think this is pretty universal for people; most people will look at a wishlist or gift list and focus on something that indicates priority, and then price, and work within whatever boundary works best for them. If you know the person is on a budget or may have restrictions, consider even just giving them a list tailored to them.

Elly: Also, making a list isn't really greedy, selfish, or immature; it helps people quite a lot when they know what to get you, and can avoid a lot of unfortunate situations where you are throwing out something a person gave you that cost them real money!

Provide Pictures

Marcy: I think that when you're dealing with hobby items, whether they're gunpla, LEGOs or otherwise, providing a picture of some sort can be a huge help. Gunpla especially can be pretty confusing to people who don't really know what they're looking at, so putting a big string of numbers in front of their face doesn't really help. YOU might know the difference between the two kits, but the person shopping for you doesn't, so if you don't give them a visual cue to work off of, there might be some issues with what you end up getting.

Elly: I do think that this can be something that goes over people's heads; I'll be honest and say it has even gone over mine at times. If the item is specialized, just having the name of the item isn't always all you need. And while sometimes you can just send a link to the item off of a website to buy it from, it can still be helpful to have secondary confirmation that the thing you actually want looks like a specific thing, so that it doesn't cause confusion.

Marcy: I actually remember a time when I was buying a gift for someone and the item had two variants, which were unknown to even the person who asked for it, and the website made no mention of except during check out, meaning that I basically had to guess which of the two they actually wanted. I lucked out, thankfully.

Elly:If you have partners, family, friends, or otherwise that are asking or expecting to exchange gifts with you, just remember that telling them "I want the GQuuuuuuX kit" means basically nothing to them if they have no idea what that is. And for LEGO, I think this can also apply: just saying you want a LEGO set without a specific picture can create some confusion if there are multiple in the line, such as the One Piece or Transformers kits; even the botanicals can be kind of hard if people don't pay a lot of attention and just think "flower".

Marcy: Right. I think the second aspect here is that you're trying to fool proof the process, both in terms of bad communication on your part (IE, not telling them clearly about the specific thing you wanted by providing as much information as you can), and on their part (them not knowing what they're looking for and not being able to ask, while also just assuming that anything they get will be fine.

Consider the Source

Amazon used to be an extremely reliable, if questionably run, online store that could often solve much of the holiday shopping experience. The issue is that not only has Amazon gotten worse, but everything else around them has also gotten worse, which means that you can't rely on them as the be all end all solution to general shopping. If you haven't tried ordering anything from there lately, you might be surprised at how hard it can be to search a specific thing you're looking for without being inundated with "Sponsored" listings, knock-offs, and advertisements for unrelated things. Also, shipping speed, time, and availability has also become pretty variable and unreliable, which is a lot of words to say: you can't rely on Amazon being a solution to your gifting issues as much these days.

Instead, by looking into where people can get the things you want, you can also consider that while YOU may know how to order from those sites and be familiar with them, your loved ones are, again, not you, and thus are going to have a harder time knowing who to trust and how. Try to be clear in making your list, offer alternatives, and try to ensure that the things you're asking for can be found easily.

Elly: Yeah... especially with something like Gunpla, you'd possibly be surprised seeing the price variance on them. A kit that is normally 20 dollars might inexplicably be 50 dollars at Barnes and Noble, for example; finding them in Michaels for nearly twice their MSRP would turn off most experienced hobbyists, but people trying to do holiday shopping might not know that and end up wasting money.

Marcy: And, if you live in the US, you probably need to consider that asking for things that ship from outside of the US is a lot more complicated than it used to be, and that the people ordering things for you, either shipped to them or to you, are going to be less aware of and familiar with that issue than you might be if you're ordering overseas items for your hobby regularly. Try to not only give people options, but try to pick easy to shop with, or easy to use, websites, be informative, and try to provide as much information as you can to the person without being overwhelming.

Hopefully, taking some of this information to heart while working on your holiday wants and needs can help smooth things over with people, while also being something you can apply for yourself; when people start asking for or hinting about gifts, these tips also apply! Don't try to shop based on what you want or know, rely on what they're asking for instead, and you'll likely end up with a far more enjoyable overall holiday season!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.
